articles.title: NORDEN more than doubles Q3 profit to US$54 million
articles.summary: Danish shipping company NORDEN reported a net profit of US$54 million for the third quarter of 2026, more than double the US$26 million recorded in the corresponding period last year, supported by stronger market conditions across its Dry Cargo and Tankers businesses. The company’s quarterly net profit increased by...
articles.body: Danish shipping company NORDEN reported a net profit of US$54 million for the third quarter of 2026, more than double the US$26 million recorded in the corresponding period last year, supported by stronger market conditions across its Dry Cargo and Tankers businesses. The company’s quarterly net profit increased by approximately 108% year-on-year, while operating cash flow reached US$150 million, compared with US$96 million in the third quarter of 2025. Following the results, NORDEN raised its full-year net profit guidance to US$200–250 million, up from its previous forecast of US$180–230 million. The updated outlook includes US$79 million in vessel sales gains, unchanged from the previous quarter. During 2026, NORDEN continued adjusting its fleet portfolio in response to market developments, adding vessels to its core fleet in the Handysize and multipurpose (MPP) segments. The company also secured long-term charter agreements for MR tankers and Capesize vessels, aiming to strengthen future revenue visibility and reduce exposure to fluctuations in freight markets. Jan Rindbo, CEO of NORDEN, said the company had delivered a strong quarter across both its principal business segments, supported by the flexibility of its operating model and improved visibility for the remainder of the year. NORDEN reported a return on invested capital of 11.8%, while its estimated net asset value reached DKK 523 per share, representing an increase of 38% since the beginning of 2026. The company also announced a third-quarter shareholder distribution of US$24 million, comprising an interim dividend of DKK 2 per share and a new US$15 million share buyback programme. Despite raising its earnings outlook, NORDEN highlighted continued geopolitical uncertainty and cautioned that the timing of certain voyages could shift some earnings into 2027.

articles.title: DNV confirms feasibility of ship-based CO₂ injection concept for Atlas project
articles.summary: DNV has issued a Statement of Feasibility for a ship-based CO₂ transport and offshore injection concept being developed by Aker BP and Höegh Evi for the Atlas carbon storage project on the Norwegian Continental Shelf. The concept involves transporting liquefied CO₂ aboard specialised shuttle carriers and injecting it...
articles.body: DNV has issued a Statement of Feasibility for a ship-based CO₂ transport and offshore injection concept being developed by Aker BP and Höegh Evi for the Atlas carbon storage project on the Norwegian Continental Shelf. The concept involves transporting liquefied CO₂ aboard specialised shuttle carriers and injecting it directly into subsea storage reservoirs, potentially eliminating the need for new onshore facilities, cross-border pipelines and permanent offshore structures. The Atlas project is designed to initially inject up to 6 million tonnes of CO₂ annually, with an estimated total storage capacity of 150 million tonnes. Aker BP is targeting the start of injection operations in 2031, subject to future investment decisions. DNV’s assessment focused on the offshore infrastructure required to transfer CO₂ from the vessels into subsea injection wells. The classification and assurance organisation identified technical challenges and uncertainties but concluded that these were manageable at the current development stage. The evaluation was conducted using DNV’s technology qualification methodology and follows earlier Approvals in Principle covering Höegh Evi’s liquefied CO₂ carrier and floating CO₂ reception and conditioning terminal concepts. Under the proposed transport system, captured CO₂ from European industrial facilities would be collected, processed and liquefied at a floating terminal before being transported to the offshore storage site. The terminal is designed to provide between 40,000 and 80,000 cubic metres of intermediate storage capacity, while individual shuttle carriers could transport up to 50,000 cubic metres of CO₂ per voyage. At the Atlas site, offshore transfer equipment and subsea pipelines would enable CO₂ to be injected directly into the reservoir. The project is being developed by Aker BP, which holds an 80% interest in the Atlas storage licence, alongside ORLEN with the remaining 20%. In October 2026, Aker BP and Höegh Evi were awarded €223 million in support from the EU Innovation Fund for the proposed cross-border CO₂ transport and storage network. The funding remains subject to a Final Investment Decision, currently targeted for 2028. The concept could also be considered for Aker BP’s Poseidon CO₂ storage licence on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, where a similar subsea development approach is under evaluation.
takeaways: DNV has issued a Statement of Feasibility for a ship-based CO₂ transport and offshore injection concept being developed by Aker BP and Höegh Evi for the Atlas carbon storage project on the Norwegian Continental Shelf.
The Atlas project is designed to initially inject up to 6 million tonnes of CO₂ annually, with an estimated total storage capacity of 150 million tonnes.
Aker BP is targeting the start of injection operations in 2031, subject to future investment decisions.

articles.title: SEA-LNG and MAMII sign four-year partnership on methane emissions
articles.summary: SEA-LNG and the Methane Abatement in Maritime Innovation Initiative (MAMII) have signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen technical cooperation on methane emissions from LNG-fuelled vessels. Under the agreement, MAMII will serve as a technical knowledge partner within SEA-LNG’s delegation at...
articles.body: SEA-LNG and the Methane Abatement in Maritime Innovation Initiative (MAMII) have signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen technical cooperation on methane emissions from LNG-fuelled vessels. Under the agreement, MAMII will serve as a technical knowledge partner within SEA-LNG’s delegation at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), contributing expertise on methane measurement methodologies, emissions monitoring and abatement technologies. The partnership will also see MAMII representatives participate in IMO technical working groups, correspondence groups and related discussions under SEA-LNG’s coordination. The collaboration builds on an existing relationship between the two organisations and follows MAMII’s research into methane reduction technologies, including trials involving plasma-catalytic systems and methane-oxidation catalysts. According to the initiative, these trials have produced promising preliminary results. Steve Esau, Chief Operating Officer of SEA-LNG, said the partnership would strengthen the organisation’s technical engagement at the IMO and contribute to policy discussions supported by industry data and research. Panos Mitrou, Chair of MAMII and Senior Vice President for Shipping Strategy at Lloyd’s Register, highlighted the importance of technical evidence in developing measures to address maritime emissions. The agreement follows SEA-LNG’s initial participation in IMO meetings as a non-governmental organisation with consultative status and comes ahead of further Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) discussions in November. MAMII, launched and led by Safetytech Accelerator, brings together maritime companies, LNG stakeholders and technology developers to support the development and adoption of methane measurement and reduction solutions for LNG-powered ships.

articles.title: Port of Virginia orders 10 electric straddle carriers from Kalmar
articles.summary: Kalmar has secured an order for 10 fully electric straddle carriers from the Port of Virginia in the United States. articles.body: Kalmar has secured an order for 10 fully electric straddle carriers from the Port of Virginia in the United States. The equipment will be deployed at Norfolk International Terminals (NIT), the port’s largest container terminal. The order was recorded in Kalmar’s third-quarter 2026 order intake. Deliveries are scheduled to be completed during the third quarter of 2027. The new electric straddle carriers will support the port’s efforts to reduce emissions and improve operational safety. The Port of Virginia aims to achieve net-zero Scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions by 2040. Electric equipment for Norfolk International Terminals The straddle carriers will feature lithium-ion batteries designed for heavy-duty operations. According to Kalmar, the equipment can operate for up to 600 minutes. Each machine will also include the Kalmar Collision Warning System. The technology uses visual and audible alerts to warn operators about potential collision risks. “Integrating these fully electric Kalmar straddle carriers with the Collision Warning System into our operations is a vital step in our journey to create safer and more sustainable operations,” said Patrick Jefferson, Director of Operations at Norfolk International Terminals. NIT is undergoing an expansion that will increase its annual terminal capacity to 3.6 million TEUs. Following completion of the equipment delivery, the terminal is expected to have more than 90 semi-automated stacking cranes and 113 Kalmar hybrid straddle carriers, alongside the newly ordered electric equipment. The Port of Virginia also operates Virginia International Gateway (VIG), another semi-automated container terminal. Kalmar and the Port of Virginia have maintained a commercial relationship since 2007. The latest order extends their cooperation as the port continues investing in container-handling equipment and terminal operations. The financial value of the order was not disclosed.
takeaways: Kalmar has secured an order for 10 fully electric straddle carriers from the Port of Virginia in the United States.
The equipment will be deployed at Norfolk International Terminals (NIT), the port’s largest container terminal.
The order was recorded in Kalmar’s third-quarter 2026 order intake.

articles.body: Kalmar has received an order from Tropical Shipping for a hybrid straddle carrier and a reachstacker for its container terminal in Riviera Beach, Florida. The order was recorded in Kalmar’s third-quarter 2026 order intake, with delivery of both machines scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The new straddle carrier will be the first hybrid model in Tropical Shipping’s fleet. The company selected the equipment as part of its efforts to manage fuel consumption, maintenance expenses and emissions. The hybrid straddle carrier will be equipped with MyKalmar INSIGHT, a digital fleet management solution that provides equipment performance and operational information. Expanding terminal equipment capacity Following the addition of the new machines, Tropical Shipping’s fleet will comprise 29 Kalmar straddle carriers and 25 reachstackers. The company said the investment would support operational efficiency at its Florida terminal, which serves its Caribbean shipping network. “Adding our first hybrid straddle carrier supports our goal of managing fuel and maintenance costs effectively over the machine’s lifetime while continuing to deliver reliable service across our terminal operations,” said Douglas Cowper, Vice President of Operations at Tropical Shipping. Cowper also highlighted the company’s existing relationship with Kalmar and the benefits of sourcing both equipment types from the same supplier. The order continues the cooperation between the two companies as Tropical Shipping expands its container-handling capabilities. Kalmar did not disclose the financial value of the contract.

articles.title: Hellmann expands US logistics network with three new branches
articles.summary: Hellmann Worldwide Logistics has expanded its presence in the United States with three new branches in Indianapolis, the Columbus metropolitan area and the San Francisco Bay Area. articles.body: Hellmann Worldwide Logistics has expanded its presence in the United States with three new branches in Indianapolis, the Columbus metropolitan area and the San Francisco Bay Area. The expansion brings the company’s US network to 12 branches and forms part of its Forward2030 growth strategy. Each location will focus on specific industries while supporting customers through international and domestic logistics services. Hellmann, which established its US operations in 1988, is strengthening its coverage across sea freight, air freight and road transportation. New branches target key industries The Indianapolis branch is already operational and focuses on the automotive industry. It supports Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers with international ocean and air freight services, alongside domestic road transportation. Meanwhile, the new office in the Columbus metropolitan area of Ohio will serve customers in the fashion and retail sectors. The third location, near San Francisco International Airport, will focus on technology-related industries. These include semiconductors, electronics, cloud infrastructure and renewable energy. Together, the three branches will expand Hellmann’s ability to provide industry-specific logistics services across major US manufacturing and commercial markets. “The United States plays a pivotal role in our global growth strategy,” said Mario Stecher, Managing Director US at Hellmann Worldwide Logistics. Stecher added that the new locations would strengthen the company’s ability to serve customers in strategically important markets. The expansion also supports Hellmann’s US Accelerator Program, which aims to develop the company’s regional operations through targeted investment and industry expertise. Peter Hüwel, Regional CEO Americas at Hellmann Worldwide Logistics, said the program combines the company’s international network with local market knowledge to support further growth. The new branches extend Hellmann’s US footprint as the company continues to develop integrated logistics solutions for customers across its international network.

articles.title: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?
articles.summary: In September we borrowed a Led Zeppelin title to describe China’s crude stockpile, a levee holding backthe import shortfall created by the closure of Hormuz. One month on, the wateris still falling, Gulf crude has rambled on around the Strait, and the questionis what it will cost to rebuild. China’s customs...
articles.body: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight? in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 In September we borrowed a Led Zeppelin title to describe China’s crude stockpile, a levee holding backthe import shortfall created by the closure of Hormuz. One month on, the wateris still falling, Gulf crude has rambled on around the Strait, and the questionis what it will cost to rebuild. China’s customs crudeimports were 9.03 mbpd in September, broadly flat on August, while refineryruns climbed to 13.99 mbpd, the highest since March. Hence China drew on itsstocks for the fourth time in five months, a net 0.60 mbpd after crude exports (Figure1). Of the 121.5 million barrels built by April, only 31 million remain. At theMay to September pace of 0.59 mbpd, that would be gone by late November.Arrivals picked up in October, but those cargoes were bought in the summer, andwith Brent around US$ 100 since early September, the refill is likely to slow. From the Red Sea to the relay: two bypasses in six months The levee was needed because the Gulf’s main exit closed. Our data shows that crude loaded directly inside the Strait of Hormuz fell from about 14 mbpd in January and February to under 1 mbpd in September. China felt it first, with customs imports dropping from 12.0 mbpd in January and February to 7.1 mbpd in June, and the gap was met from tanks. However, Gulf crude kept moving, and it changed route twice. Between March and July the Red Sea carried the load, with Saudi crude piped across the Peninsula and loaded at Yanbu and Rabigh, a route that peaked at about 4.3 mbpd in June, against about 0.8 mbpd before the war. The attack on the East-West pipeline in August threw a spanner in the works. The weight shifted back east, and crude now crosses the Strait on tankers, some of them on dark transits, before being transferred ship to ship onto VLCCs off Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and Sohar. This relay grew from almost nothing in February to about 5 mbpd in September, while loadings at Fujairah’s berths and Oman’s own ports carried a further 3.9 mbpd. By September, loadings at the hub ports had risen to about 8.5 mbpd, five times their 2025 level, and briefly ran close to 12 mbpd in the last week of the month. Where the barrels went Meanwhile, the cheapest barrels have gone. After the US blockade in April, Iranian crude largely stopped leaving the Gulf, and the Iranian barrels floating off Malaysia and Singapore are close to exhausted by our count (Figure 2). China’s choice narrows to its stockpile or Gulf crude. Why has freight not decided where Asia buys? VLCC earnings on the MEG/China route (TD3C) moved from parity with West Africa/China (TD15) in January and February to 4.2 times TD15 in May, and averaged US$ 1.02 million/day TCE in September, 17.5 times their 2025 average (Figure 3). On earnings alone, the Atlantic looked the obvious alternative, unless the crude could be loaded outside the Strait, on the Gulf of Oman route (TD34). However, earnings overstate what the buyer pays. At the Baltic’s standard speeds of 13 knots laden and 12 knots in ballast, a VLCC needs about 46 days for the round voyage from Ras Tanura to Ningbo, against about 76 days from West Africa, so the lower daily rate on TD15 is billed for longer. Take a VLCC carrying about 2 million barrels to Ningbo in September. Loaded at Ras Tanura, inside the Strait, the cargo paid about US$ 52 million in freight, or US$ 26/bbl. Loaded in West Africa it paid about US$ 35 million, or US$ 17.5/bbl, even though TD3C earned 2.5 times as much per day as TD15. Loaded at Mina al Fahal in Oman, outside the Strait, it paid about US$ 30 million, or US$ 15/bbl, the cheapest of the three. By October the order was the same and the gaps wider: about US$ 34/bbl from Ras Tanura, US$ 28 from West Africa and US$ 19 from Mina al Fahal. Furthermore, as the relay off Fujairah, priced on TD34, took over after the pipeline attack, China’s imports recovered with it. The TD3C premium, in turn, priced the difficulty of leaving the Gulf. Whenever a route out of the Gulf opened, Asia bought. Our numbers show who paid that premium: cargoes loaded inside the Strait, on TD3C, and buyers avoided those wherever they could. A VLCC loading in the Gulf of Oman, meanwhile, cost less to send to China than one loading in West Africa. Crude prices set how much it bought: Brent rose from US$ 72.48 before the war to an intraday high of about US$ 126 on 30 April, and Chinese buying only recovered once it fell below US$ 80 in the summer. Gulf producers’ discounts, and the fit of Gulf medium sour grades with Asia’s complex refineries, explain why buyers returned so quickly. What it means for tonnage Every cargo that crosses the Strait on one tanker and is reloaded onto another off Oman ties up two vessels and adds waiting time at the transfer point. September showed the first sustained sign of demand pulling on that system, as freight for VLCCs loading in the Gulf of Oman (TD34) tripled m-o-m, faster than TD3C inside the Strait. Attacks on tankers crossing the Strait at the end of September did not stop the trade. In October the shortage reached the Atlantic. The number of VLCCs ballasting towards West Africa, Brazil and the US Gulf fell from about 85 a week in early September to 50 to 54 since mid-October, while transfers off Oman ran at their limits. TD15 rose 60% m-o-m in Worldscale, against 26% for TD34, taking West African earnings to US$ 667,000/day. The bill comes due The September loadings now on the water will reach China in October and November, just as the stock build runs out. China is still buying from the Atlantic, with 19 VLCCs fixed from Brazil and West Africa to China in the last ten days of October, most of them loading in November. Should the transfer network off Oman keep pace, Gulf crude will carry the refill and keep drawing tonnage east, supporting earnings on both routes. Should it falter, China will have to choose between drawing deeper into a stockpile estimated at more than a billion barrels and buying from further away, at a higher freight cost per barrel. Either way, the cost of moving a barrel to Asia has become part of the price of the barrel itself. articles.title: Tanker Orders Leading Newbuilding Activity With Prices Expected to Remain High Throughout 2027
articles.summary: Tanker ordering activity has been leading the latest surge of contracting, despite high prices, Banchero Costa said in a new research report focused on newbuilding. More specifically, the shipbroker noted that “the shipbuilding market has moved from an ordering boom into a delivery wave. The total orderbook for...
articles.body: Tanker Orders Leading Newbuilding Activity With Prices Expected to Remain High Throughout 2027 in Hellenic Shipping News 31/10/2026 T anker ordering activity has been leading the latest surge of contracting, despite high prices, Banchero Costa said in a new research report focused on newbuilding. More specifically, the shipbroker noted that “the shipbuilding market has moved from an ordering boom into a delivery wave. The total orderbook for bulkcarriers, tankers, LNG and LPG carriers and containerships stands at 179.1 mln CGT, 25.0% more than a year earlier (143.3 mln CGT) and the largest in the last 20 years. Containerships account for 38% of it, ahead of bulkcarriers (18%) and LNG carriers (16%). Relative to the fleet it is largest for containerships (43.5%), LNG carriers (40.9%), LPG carriers (38.5%) and crude tankers (29.3%), against 14.2% for bulkcarriers. The orderbook for bulkcarriers and crude and product tankers stands at 2,700 ships and 326.5 mln DWT, or 19.1% of the fleet, 41% more than a year ago and 2.7 times its 2021 level. Yard capacity is the main constraint. Chinese yards hold 75% of the bulkcarrier and tanker orderbook and are scheduled to deliver 89.1 mln DWT of these ships in 2028, against their record of 62.6 mln DWT in 2011”. According to Banchero Costa, “contracting has been driven by tankers. In Jan-Sep 2026, 267 crude tankers of 67.0 mln DWT were ordered (+267.7% y-o-y), including 172 VLCCs, while bulkcarrier ordering held steady (+4.7% in DWT terms). 83 LNG carriers of 13.12 mln CBM were ordered, against 35 of 2.94 mln CBM a year earlier, and 519 containerships of 4.05 mln TEU (+11.7%), 89% of them at Chinese yards”. Additionally, “newbuilding prices are firm for tankers and bulkcarriers but softer for large containerships and LNG carriers. In Sep 2026 a VLCC was assessed at USD 131.0 mln (+7.4% y-o-y) and a Capesize at USD 79.0 mln (+3.9%), while a 20,000 TEU containership eased to USD 210.4 mln (-4.8%) and a 180,000 CBM LNG carrier to USD 242.0 mln (-3.3%). We expect tanker newbuilding prices to stay firm into 2027, with the main yards full until 2029, but see limited room for further gains as new Chinese capacity comes on stream. With 33% of this year’s contracting (in CGT) at new or revived yards, the main risks are delays and the 2028 delivery peak”, the shipbroker said. THE ORDERBOOK: LARGEST FOR CONTAINERSHIPS, GAS CARRIERS AND TANKERS Banchero Costa added that “the orderbook is large in every cargo sector, but its size relative to the fleet differs widely. Bulkcarriers of 20,000 DWT and over have 1,449 ships and 145.3 mln DWT on order (14.2% of the trading fleet), crude tankers of 60,000 DWT and over 574 ships and 135.4 mln DWT (29.3%), coated product tankers of 30,000-119,999 DWT 677 ships and 45.9 mln DWT (20.7%), and IMO I/II chemical tankers of 1,000-41,999 DWT 540 ships (20.2%). Containerships and gas carriers have the largest orderbooks relative to their fleets. 1,641 fully cellular containerships of 14.6 mln TEU are on order, equal to 43.5% of the fleet, and the ULCS orderbook equals 87% of the ULCS fleet. For LNG carriers the ratio is 40.9% (350 ships of 54.9 mln CBM) and for LPG carriers 38.5% (320 ships of 21.4 mln CBM), with the VLGC orderbook at 44.6% of the VLGC fleet”. Meanwhile, during the past week, Banchero Costa noted that “newbuilding activity this week was broad-based, with significant contracting across the bulk carrier, container, tanker, gas carrier and offshore sectors. The bulk carrier sector was particularly notable for a major grain transportation programme involving COSCO Shipping Bulk. In the bulk carrier sector, COSCO Shipping Bulk reportedly arranged a programme for 16x 87,000 dwt bulk carriers at Fujian Mawei, priced at approximately USD 49.5 million each, with deliveries scheduled between March 2029 and September 2035. In the container sector, HMM reportedly contracted 7x 13,000 teu containerships at Hyundai Samho, priced at approximately USD 180.1 million each, with deliveries scheduled for March 2028. Danaos Shipping also reportedly contracted 2x 9,200 teu containerships at Shanghai Waigaoqiao, priced at approximately USD 109 million each, with deliveries scheduled for June and December 2029. articles.body: Suezmax Tanker sales surge 35% amid high VLCC demand in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 A strong VLCC market this year is boosting Suezmax Tanker demand. Suezmax sales activity has picked up considerably in recent months, with sales so far this year up 35%, reaching 124 sales compared to 92 sales over the same period last year. Buyers have continued to transact even as values have climbed, pointing to strong sector demand. Both values and timecharter rates are now at an all-time high, with one year timecharter rates four times higher than this time last year, adding to the momentum behind sales and keeping buyer and seller interest firmly focused on the sector. The average age of vessels sold is 15 years. On the buying side, Greece has been the biggest buyer with 21% of purchases, followed by the UAE with 15% and China in third place with 8%. Greece has also been active on the selling side, accounting for 33% of sales, including nine Suezmax vessels sold by Dynacom this year. China is in second place with 9% of sales and Belgium in third with 6%, as CMB.Tech and Exmar offloaded eight vessels combined. Notable recent sales include the Suezmax Achilleas (158,400 DWT, Jun 2010, Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan) sold by Sun Enterprises for USD 98.0 mil, VV Value USD 100.47 mil. Also the Suezmax Maran Poseidon (158,300 DWT, Jan 2010, Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan) sold by Maran Tankers for USD 98.5 mil, VV Value USD 101.88 mil. What’s Driving the Demand? As VLCC values have risen this year, it has inadvertently pushed up demand for the considerably cheaper Suezmax Tanker segment. As attention has transferred from VLCCs to Suezmax Tankers, strong buying and higher earnings have pushed values up significantly across all size ranges, narrowing the price gap between the two, though not as sharply as VLCC values have risen. Older Suezmax vessels have seen the biggest gains, with a 15YO 160,000 DWT Suezmax up c.134.58% since the start of the year, from USD 45.6 mil to USD 106.97 mil. The scale of the move for older tonnage shows how quickly pricing across the age spectrum has reset in a matter of months. Earnings have moved in the same direction. One-year timecharter rates are up by 301% year on year, from 40,151 USD/day to 161,054 USD/day. Disruptions to normal trading patterns have made reliable tonnage harder to find, and with demand for Suezmax Tankers rising at the same time, owners have been able to command significantly higher rates for longer commitments. A one-year timecharter now locks in earnings at a level that would have been hard to imagine twelve months ago, which helps explain why values have followed rates higher. Sellers are also looking to capitalise on these gains, with the combination of firm earnings and rising asset values shaping activity in the sector. Part of the appeal of Suezmax Tankers is their versatility. Unlike VLCCs, they can transit the Suez Canal fully laden, which opens up a direct route between the Middle East, the Mediterranean and Europe and avoids the longer passage around the Cape of Good Hope. The Tankers’ size also gives them access to a wider range of ports and terminals than VLCCs, giving charterers more flexibility in the trades they can serve. With VLCC values and earnings already elevated and vessels in short supply due to strong demand, Suezmaxes offer a more flexible and cheaper alternative within the Tanker market. Activity in the sector will be one to watch in the coming weeks. Source: Veson Nautical Tops 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: China charts course for green corridors
articles.summary: China is emerging as an influential player in the global green shipping corridor movement, leveraging its dominance in green fuel production, battery technology and maritime infrastructure to take a leading role in efforts to decarbonise international shipping. Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value...
articles.body: China charts course for green corridors in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 31/10/2026 C hina is emerging as an influential player in the global green shipping corridor movement, leveraging its dominance in green fuel production, battery technology and maritime infrastructure to take a leading role in efforts to decarbonise international shipping. Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value chain, the country still faces significant challenges if it is to convert ambition into commercially viable zero-emission trade routes. A report from the Global Maritime Forum on China’s progress with green shipping corridors noted that China was involved in at least 21 green corridor initiatives as of June 2026, representing “nearly a fifth of the global green corridor portfolio”. According to the report, China possesses strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks needed to successfully develop green shipping corridors: viable zero-emission fuel pathways, cross-value-chain collaboration and an enabling policy environment. Customer demand remains the weakest link. “China holds strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks necessary to successfully realise green corridors,” the report said. It adds that the country is positioning itself “as a leading supplier of three zero-emission fuels and technologies central to the advancement of green corridors: methanol, ammonia, and electric batteries”. That strength is built on China’s rapid expansion in green methanol and ammonia production, coupled with its emergence as a global leader in marine battery technology. The report highlights the country’s “low cost and early availability of green methanol and ammonia” and its position “at the forefront of marine battery development” as key competitive advantages. At the same time, China benefits from “innovative commercial partnerships and knowledge-sharing platforms across the value chain” and “rapidly strengthening policies related to green hydrogen”. Green avenues The report says that successfully developing green corridors could help China scale strategic hydrogen and battery industries, gain market share in a global bunker market worth approximately $100bn and participate in a wider maritime decarbonisation investment pipeline valued at between $1tn and $2tn. It could also support as many as four million green jobs while helping future-proof Chinese shipyards and maritime labour against the energy transition. However, the report stresses that major barriers remain. For example, there are gaps in both “soft” and “hard” infrastructure, including fuel certification systems, bunkering networks and charging infrastructure. It also points to the risk of competition for green ammonia from domestic industries, difficulties maintaining alignment across corridor partnerships, high costs associated with alternative fuels and battery-electric vessels, and what it describes as “fragmented global demand for zero-emission shipping services”. But the overarching challenge is economic. While China may currently offer some of the lowest-cost green methanol and ammonia globally, those fuels remain significantly more expensive than conventional marine fuels. Likewise, battery-powered vessels still carry substantial capital cost premiums. The report warns that customer demand has not developed at the same pace as supply-side initiatives. While some cargo owners are willing to pay higher freight rates for lower-carbon transport, willingness to absorb green fuel premiums remains inconsistent across markets. This creates uncertainty for project developers, shipowners and fuel producers attempting to make large-scale investments. Against this backdrop, the report’s recommendations section focuses on a set of practical measures that could help move Chinese corridors from planning into operation. Points for success The first recommendation calls for accelerated development of infrastructure supporting methanol, ammonia and battery-electric shipping. The report argues that progress is needed in both certification frameworks and physical logistics networks. “This can be split into two focal points: soft infrastructure, aligning fuel projects with global certification standards, and hard infrastructure, the rollout of physical fuel transportation and bunkering networks,” the report noted. “Both are necessary to connect China’s green fuel production with the global shipping sector.” Alignment with international standards is viewed as particularly important for routes linking China and Europe. The report notes that compatibility with the EU’s Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin framework will be essential if shipping companies are to maximise regulatory compliance benefits under European legislation. The second recommendation focuses on governance and collaboration. Drawing on lessons from green corridor projects around the world, the report says successful initiatives tend to share several traits, including clear governance structures, technology-focused targets, detailed feasibility studies and comprehensive implementation roadmaps. The report also suggests that China can shorten development timelines by building on partnerships that already exist around fuel production, bunkering and offtake agreements. Rather than creating entirely new structures, corridor developers may be able to use existing commercial relationships as the foundation for broader decarbonisation projects. A third recommendation centres on policy intervention to close the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels. “Both national and international policy action will be needed to support the success of green corridors,” the report says. The authors argue that corridors connected to Europe already benefit from demand signals created by the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. They also point to growing domestic support mechanisms in China, including green fuel incentives and hydrogen pilot programmes that could lower fuel costs and encourage early deployment. Creating partnerships Looking ahead, the report suggests there is scope for bilateral and plurilateral cooperation with major trading partners including the EU, Singapore, Australia and the United States. Mechanisms such as H2Global are highlighted as potential models for supporting green fuel deployment across international trade routes. The final recommendation addresses what may prove the most difficult challenge: creating customer demand. “Customer demand can be leveraged by targeting the shipping sectors that have demonstrated a higher willingness to pay and/or aggregating mechanisms,” the report argues. The authors recommend focusing on first-mover industries with established climate commitments, particularly participants in the iron ore, vehicle and container sectors. Engaging cargo-owner alliances such as the Zero-Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance could also help consolidate demand and improve willingness to pay for green shipping services. Meanwhile, domestic policy measures aimed at reducing shipping carbon intensity among China’s state-owned enterprises may provide an additional source of early demand. In its conclusion, the report presents a clear assessment of China’s position within the global maritime energy transition. “With a portfolio that represents nearly one-fifth of global initiatives and international collaboration as a national priority, China is well-positioned to lead the development of green shipping corridors,” the report concludes. It adds that China has “clear strengths across three of the four key building blocks required to make green corridors a success”, citing fuel availability, policy support and supply-chain collaboration. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value chain, the country still faces significant challenges if it is to convert ambition into commercially viable zero-emission trade routes.
Customer demand remains the weakest link.
“China holds strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks necessary to successfully realise green corridors,” the report said.

articles.body: Sanctioned Iran-Linked Tankers Went Dark Over Gulf of Oman Cables as the IRGC Threatened Them in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 Seven Cable Systems Run Through the Corridor The waters off Oman’s Batinah coast carry one of the densest concentrations of undersea cables in the region. Seven systems pass through the corridors where the three tankers operated, namely 2Africa, Bay of Bengal Gateway (BBG), Asia Africa Europe-1 (AAE-1), the Oman Australia Cable (OAC), Europe India Gateway (EIG), Transworld (TW1), and SeaMeWe-4. Between them, these cables connect Oman, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Egypt, and Europe, with OAC running onward to Australia. Their owners include Meta, Vodafone, Orange, AT&T, Verizon, BT, China Mobile, China Telecom, Reliance Jio, Omantel, e&, and many of the region’s major telecom operators. Damage here would ripple well beyond the Gulf. Loops, U-Turns, and Days in the Dark A Loop and an 86-Hour Blackout Off Sohar On October 14 and 15, CELESTIAL SEA (IMO 9397030), a U.S.-sanctioned, Iran-flagged products tanker, drifted in a loop for 4.3 hours at 0 to 1.4 knots, 0.65 nautical miles from the 2Africa corridor. On October 15, it went dark inside the 2Africa and BBG corridors off Sohar. It stayed dark for 86 hours and came back transmitting only about 9 nautical miles from where it went dark. When it reappeared on October 19, it made a U-turn above BBG and then anchored off Shinas. The tanker was in ballast throughout, according to Vortexa data. A Laden Gas Carrier Turns Away From Malaysia A U.S.-sanctioned very large gas carrier (VLGC) was anchored next to CELESTIAL SEA. On October 23, the VLGC left Shinas for Pasir Gudang in Malaysia, laden with about 494,500 barrels of LPG, according to Vortexa data. Ten hours later, it slowed below 3 knots for 42 minutes inside the 2Africa corridor, with OAC and BBG 2.5 to 4 nautical miles away. It then turned 180 degrees back toward Oman, away from its destination, and went dark about 2 nautical miles from AAE-1. As of October 28, it had been dark for five days. Ten Days Loitering Between Jask and Chabahar The third tanker, an Iran-flagged very large crude carrier (VLCC) in ballast according to Vortexa data, loitered at under 1 knot for about 10 days in Iran’s EEZ between Jask and Chabahar, 0.4 to 3 nautical miles from the EIG, TW1, BBG, and SeaMeWe-4 routes. It went dark repeatedly, including for 33 hours from October 17. On October 18, it met an Iran-flagged vessel with no IMO number. It has been dark since October 26. Three Tankers With Direct Ties to Iran’s State and Military All three tankers are part of Iran’s sanctioned oil trade. CELESTIAL SEA was sanctioned by OFAC in April 2025, under its former name HARMONY, as part of the fleet of a UAE-based operator whose vessels moved oil for the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and, in 2023, for the Iranian military, according to the U.S. Treasury. The operator also worked with associates of a Houthi financial official. The tanker has used an Iranian call sign and an Iranian MMSI, and it swapped identities with another tanker in August 2025. In May, U.S. Marines boarded it in the Gulf of Oman on suspicion of trying to break the U.S. blockade. The VLCC flies Iran’s flag and is operated by the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC), the state tanker company. Treasury sanctioned NITC in 2020, together with the Petroleum Ministry and NIOC, for funding the IRGC Quds Force. The VLCC’s registered owner is also listed by the UK and EU. The tanker has broadcast two other names and has met the same Iran-flagged vessel about nine times since August. The VLGC was sanctioned in April 2026, together with its Panama-based owner, for carrying about two million barrels of Iranian LPG since early 2025, according to Treasury. It changed its MMSI and call sign in May and June, took on a Vietnamese operator, and was dark for 877 hours in August and September. At the Shinas anchorage, both the VLGC and CELESTIAL SEA met other vessels. A Fishing-Support Vessel Worked the Same Cables The pattern is not confined to the sanctioned tanker fleet. A 34-meter Iran-flagged general cargo vessel that Windward tags as part of a fishing support fleet resumed transmitting on October 5 in the offshore Gulf of Oman southeast of Jask, in an area it had never entered in its AIS record since November 2024. After a stop about one kilometer off the Iranian Makran coast on October 8, it went dark for almost twelve days in the same area. From October 21 to 24, it loitered at 0.1 to 0.5 knots along the EIG and TW1 routes, moving back up-current at about 3 knots and drifting again, passing over EIG on October 22 and holding 0.4 to 1.7 nautical miles from TW1 for roughly 30 hours on October 23 and 24. On October 25, it crossed FALCON and the UAE-Iran cable off Jask, then sailed north into Iranian waters. It has been dark since October 26. Its ownership is opaque. The owner and manager operate only this vessel, and its beneficial owner has been unknown since August 2025. Windward assesses its IUU fishing risk as High. Nothing public ties the company to the Iranian state. Two things are worth noting alongside that. Fishing in Iranian waters requires a licence from the state fisheries company Shilat, per FAO and UNEP. And the IRGC Navy has organized fishermen and their boats into a naval Basij that its commander described as a shadow navy, in which people enter the battle with their own vessels. Iran has used civilian and commercial hulls for intelligence collection before. The IRISL-owned SAVIZ and BEHSHAD, both registered as cargo ships, served as IRGC intelligence platforms passing targeting data to the Houthis. On October 6, U.S. forces destroyed an Iranian-linked dhow in the Gulf of Oman that CENTCOM said was conducting surveillance on U.S. Navy ships, and the IRGC has turned to unarmed spotters on small boats to identify targets. The area is a busy fishing ground. What does not fit that explanation is a small vessel with a concealed beneficial owner working slowly along two cable routes in waters it had never visited, during the weeks the IRGC was threatening those cables. Iran Threatened the Cables in the Same Weeks The three tankers worked the cable corridors in the same weeks Iran threatened the cables. On October 12, two days before CELESTIAL SEA’s loop, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables and data centers across the region could be attacked if the war resumes. On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said seven major internet cables run under Hormuz and that this time Iran’s response would be much harsher. On October 21, Yadollah Javani, political deputy to the IRGC chief commander, warned that attacks on Iranian infrastructure could bring retaliation against the Hormuz cables, according to Tasnim. On October 23, the day the VLGC slowed and turned back on 2Africa, two senior Iranian security officials noted that Tehran has detailed plans to target the Gulf’s undersea cables if the U.S. and Israel attack Iran again, and would try to prevent repairs to prolong the outage. Iran already uses merchant vessels for intelligence and military operations. The IRGC used two cargo ships belonging to the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Shipping Lines (IRISL) off Yemen to support the Houthis, including passing them targeting data and vessel tracks. Earlier this month, two other sanctioned Iran-linked tankers drifted for days over the same corridors. Iran-affiliated channels have also circulated an AI-generated video threatening to cut the Gulf’s cables, pushed by accounts assessed as troll operations. The provenance is unestablished, but the amplification places the threat in the information space alongside the official statements. Why Cargo Logistics Don’t Explain the Moves Vessels waiting off Shinas sit near the cables anyway, but cargo logistics don’t explain these moves. The VLCC and CELESTIAL SEA were empty, so their days of loitering were not floating storage. The VLGC was laden with a cargo already ordered to Malaysia, and it turned back off Muscat, far from the U.S. blockade line, right after slowing on the 2Africa corridor. CELESTIAL SEA went dark over two corridors and came back transmitting 86 hours later only 9 nautical miles away, rather than waiting at the anchorage. The fishing-support vessel carried no cargo rationale at all. It drifted at under half a knot along two cable routes in an area outside its two-year operating history, then left. For vessels from networks that already work for Iran’s state and military, that fits the profile of mapping the cable routes, or of placing charges or mines on them while dark, ahead of the attacks Tehran says it has planned. What to Watch Three of four tankers remain dark, and where and when they reappear will show whether the cable corridors were the destination or a stop along the way. Further loitering by sanctioned Iran-linked tankers over the Batinah corridors, especially alongside new IRGC statements on the cables, would confirm a pattern rather than a coincidence. Source: Windward 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: GMS Week 44 – Buyers Raise The Stakes in Weekly Demolition Reports 31/10/2026 Last week’s recovery in dry freight offered recycling buyers little encouragement. This week, however, sentiment has improved across the sub-continent, with recyclers showing greater willingness to compete for available tonnage. Bangladesh continues to lead the market, while Pakistan and India are also displaying renewed confidence. Despite improving buying interest, the shortage of suitable recycling candidates persists as owners continue to benefit from attractive trading alternatives. The Strait of Hormuz supplied another reminder of the fragile security environment surrounding Gulf shipping. A tanker was attacked near Khasab, Oman, on October 29, reportedly sustaining an engine-room fire before resuming its voyage. The incident renewed concerns over passage security and insurance costs. For ageing tanker owners, disrupted trading patterns and restricted effective vessel availability continue to support employment opportunities rather than encourage recycling decisions. Oil markets responded to the renewed uncertainty. Brent advanced above USD 117 per barrel on Friday, while WTI approached USD 104 as concerns over Middle Eastern supplies persisted. Elevated energy costs continue to pressure recycling operations and steel production, particularly across the sub-continent. Yet the same uncertainty can support tanker earnings, keeping older vessels commercially attractive for longer than recyclers would prefer. Dry freight offered mixed signals. The Baltic Dry Index edged higher from 2,693 last Thursday to 2,712 on October 29, supported by Capesizes strengthening to 4,090. Panamaxes, however, weakened to 1,921, while Supramaxes eased to 1,870. The divergence suggests that pressure is emerging in selected vessel segments without producing a broader deterioration in earnings. For recycling buyers, the prospect of additional candidates remains encouraging, but there is still little evidence of a sustained increase in supply. Steel markets provided no common direction. Indian plate recovered from an early-week decline to finish at INR 43,300 per ton, while Bangladesh remained steady at BDT 66,000. Pakistan moved in the opposite direction, falling from PKR 195,000 to PKR 188,000 per ton. Chinese steel also softened marginally to USD 307.47 per ton. Despite these uneven fundamentals, improving sentiment and persistent candidate scarcity continue to support buying interest. Physical waterfront activity continued at Alang and Chattogram, with several previously secured vessels completing delivery, while Gadani reported no new movements. Bangladesh also received potentially important regulatory news, with the reported reclassification of ship recycling from the red to orange environmental category expected to simplify future yard approvals. The development has encouraged local sentiment, although implementation and environmental compliance considerations remain important. Bangladesh retains the strongest conventional buying appetite, Pakistan is becoming increasingly constructive despite weaker steel, and India continues to benefit from specialist opportunities. Turkey remains selective within its established regional market. Across the sub-continent, buyers are showing greater confidence, but freight earnings and second-hand alternatives continue to favour owners. The willingness to buy is growing. The willingness to sell remains the missing ingredient. For Week 44 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below. articles.summary: A 41 MWh battery ferry entered service and a 151 MWh container ship design won approval this week, but the harder part is getting enough power to the quay. Battery-electric ships are moving beyond short-hop ferries. This week a 41 MWh ferry began crossing the River Plate, a fast ferry for the Strait of Gibraltar ...
articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: The grid is the limit in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 A 41 MWh battery ferry entered service and a 151 MWh container ship design won approval this week, but the harder part is getting enough power to the quay. Battery-electric ships are moving beyond short-hop ferries. This week a 41 MWh ferry began crossing the River Plate, a fast ferry for the Strait of Gibraltar was launched, an electric barge was ordered for Vietnam and a 1,700 TEU battery container ship design was approved. Each depends on power ashore. Ferries first Ferry operator Buquebus’s China Zorrilla has begun sailing between Argentina and Uruguay with a 41 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery system. It can sail for up to 1.5 hours on battery power. Norwegian battery maker Corvus Energy, which supplied the system, said it is the largest marine battery installation currently in operation on a ship. Corvus said the installation has around four times the capacity of any battery previously fitted to a commercial vessel, and that the ferry is South America’s first fully electric ship of its kind. Australian shipbuilder Incat Tasmania built the vessel. Finnish technology company Wärtsilä picked Corvus in 2023 to supply the ferry’s battery system. “This project proves that battery-electric propulsion is no longer limited to smaller ferries or short routes,” said Ole Jacob Irgens, executive vice president and head of sales at Corvus. Spanish ferry operator Baleària has launched its first fully electric fast ferry at Armon Shipyards in Gijón, Spain. The 87-metre vessel has a 14 MWh battery system and is scheduled to start sailing between Tarifa in Spain and Tangier in Morocco in summer 2027. A second ferry, now under construction, is expected to join it later that year. The two will operate along the first green corridor between Spain and Morocco. Baleària has not disclosed the launched vessel’s name. From ferries to boxes The largest battery in the week’s news is still on paper. The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has approved the concept design of a 1,700 TEU fully electric container ship developed by Hanwha Power, part of South Korean conglomerate Hanwha Group. The design runs entirely on a 151 MWh battery energy storage system, more than three times the capacity of China Zorrilla’s. The batteries sit in containerised units that can be handled and stowed like cargo containers, so they can be replaced, Hanwha Power said. The company sees the design as a potential pathway to decarbonising short-sea and regional container shipping. Even with batteries that can be lifted off like containers, the design relies on port charging to run without direct carbon emissions, Hanwha Power said. Hanwha Power has also completed the basic design of a 1,000 TEU battery-powered container ship. Batteries are heading for inland waterways too. Global sportswear company Nike has contracted French container shipping firm CMA CGM for a fully electric barge in Vietnam, which CMA CGM will operate with logistics and port operator Gemadept. The barge will link Nike’s inland drop-off location in Ho Chi Minh City with the Gemalink deep-sea terminal at Cai Mep. The plug behind the battery “Electrification shifts the energy-system burden from vessel to port,” Anthony Wiskich wrote in a working paper published this month by the Australian National University’s Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis. “Charging a large vessel during a short turnaround requires megawatt to tens-of-megawatts power, which can exceed local distribution capacity and attract severe demand-charge costs.” Baleària’s project costs more than €200 million ($223 million) and covers electrifying the ports of Tarifa and Tangier City as well as building both ferries. Nike’s barge will charge from a solar-powered station on the Gemalink terminal, CMA CGM has said. Valencia is adding grid capacity for its cargo terminals and for shore power for ships at berth. The Port Authority of Valencia (APV) has launched a tender for a new electrical substation that will double the port’s electricity supply capacity and take an estimated 20 months to build. The substation, ST2, will share between 40 megawatts (MW) and 90 MW of capacity with the existing ST1 substation, depending on which incoming power lines are used. articles.body: Rhenus has signed a ten-year agreement with the Dutch Ministry of Defence to support military logistics operations in the Netherlands. The partnership focuses on the Soesterberg Logistics Centre (LCS), which supplies materials and equipment to the country’s armed forces. Under the agreement, Rhenus will support warehouse operations and help improve supply chain processes. The partnership aims to strengthen logistics reliability and support military training, exercises and deployments. The logistics centre forms part of the Materieellogistiek Commando. It is also part of the new Soesterberg Army Base, where four separate barracks are being combined into one facility. Rhenus to support warehouse operations Rhenus will contribute its experience in warehousing, supply chain management and logistics optimisation. Meanwhile, the Ministry of Defence will provide its knowledge of military operations and requirements. Both organisations will work together to improve efficiency and strengthen logistics support. In addition, they will share expertise and develop new approaches to warehouse management. The agreement follows a relational contracting model. This approach focuses on trust, shared responsibility and transparency. It also encourages continuous improvement throughout the partnership. “The armed forces can only operate effectively if the logistics behind the scenes function excellently,” said Markus Simons, Managing Director of Rhenus Warehousing Solutions Netherlands. According to Simons, combining military knowledge with Rhenus’s logistics experience will help improve operational readiness. The Dutch Ministry of Defence also highlighted the importance of reliable supply chains. “Our military personnel must be able to rely on a logistics organisation that delivers when it matters most,” said Mark Bours, Commander of Materieellogistiek Commando at the Royal Netherlands Army’s Land Command. The partnership will support the ongoing development of logistics operations at Soesterberg. It will also allow both organisations to exchange knowledge and improve existing processes over the next ten years. The companies did not disclose the financial value of the agreement.

A potential strike threatening operations at some of the busiest container terminals in the United States has been pushed back after the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 agreed to extend negotiations through November 4. The extension provides several additional days for negotiators to reach an agreement, but the underlying labor dispute remains unresolved. October 30, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Frank Jr China's first carrier-based stealth reconnaissance and strike drone, the GJ-21, recently completed its first takeoff and landing on the Sichuan, the country's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, state news agency Xinhua reported on Friday. The trial underscores Beijing's push to integrate drone technology into its military modernisation drive, a decades-long effort in which China has developed advanced warships, fighter jets, missiles and increasingly capable unmanned systems. Xinhua hailed the test as "a breakthrough in China's amphibious assault ship programme" and said it signifies the navy's ability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large naval platforms. GJ-21 first appeared at a military parade Beijing held last year to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War Two, where it displayed different types of weapons. State tabloid the Global Times reported on Friday that GJ-21 has a substantial combat radius despite having a smaller airframe than the stealthy J-35 and J-20 fighters, citing military expert Zhang Xuefeng. "GJ-21 is also low cost and reusable. Unlike hypersonic missiles, it can be recovered and redeployed multiple times. It can also deploy small, low-cost glide-guided bombs. Under high-tempo operations, it offers greater fire delivery efficiency with better cost control," Zhang was quoted as saying. The Sichuan, the lead vessel of China's Type 076 amphibious assault ship class, was launched in December 2024 and features electromagnetic catapult and arresting technology. It can carry fixed-wing drones, helicopters and amphibious equipment. The vessel has a full-load displacement of more than 40,000 metric tons and features a full-length flight deck and twin-island superstructure. China's state television CCTV said on Friday that the indigenously developed vessel conducted consecutive sea trials in late October. It did not disclose locations of the trials. China's navy said in April that the Sichuan sailed to waters in the South China Sea for scientific testing and training missions. It said at the time the deployment was a routine test and did not aim at any specific target. (Reuters)

Strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones. "We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons," Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus. 'SEAFARERS HAVE SUFFERED MANY CASUALTIES' "We have felt it first hand, and our families have felt it too, living with the anxiety of whether a colleague will get back home," he added. More than 25 unions have now backed the strike originally called in Italy, France, Greece, Spain's Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco. On Friday, it covered major shipping hubs in Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa, as well as Morocco's Tangier Med and India's Nhava Sheva. "Seafarers have suffered many casualties — numbering in the hundreds — including both the dead and the severely injured," the Greek seafarers' union PENEN said in a statement. It said there had been 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the start of the Iran war. A series of strikes in the western Black Sea has raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia's war in Ukraine. October 30, 2026 Illustration © Yellow Boat / Adobe Stock The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that an oil leak from the Gem No. 2 tanker had been stopped, with no new leakage detected, as cleanup operations continued along coastlines affected by the spill. The oil slick is concentrated off the northern emirate of Umm Al Quwain and extends partly towards coastal areas in the neighbouring northern emirates of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah, state news agency WAM reported, citing the environment ministry. The density of marine pollution has declined markedly, it added. Authorities have temporarily closed some beaches and coastal areas as a precaution, though the ministry said this did not necessarily mean pollution had been detected at every site affected by the closures. Environment ministry teams are carrying out field surveys, monitoring and cleanup operations in coastal areas reached by the pollution, in coordination with federal and local authorities, WAM said. Authorities have not said what caused the spill, but shipping sources have told Reuters the vessel was struck by a projectile on October 9, causing a fire that was later extinguished. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout. Technical teams have repaired damaged parts of the tanker, restored some operating systems and are assessing the integrity of its structure to determine the safest way to handle it, WAM added, citing the energy ministry. The UAE also said fish and food products available in markets were safe for human consumption and that precautionary measures to protect drinking water supplies would not affect distribution. articles.summary: As gCaptain reported earlier this week, the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Wojciech Wrzesien / Shutterstock By Tom Ewing (gCaptain) – As gCaptain reported earlier this week , the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in more than 20 years. According to the Department of Transportation (DOT) , the review was completed nearly 3.7 years faster than the historical average, representing a 70% reduction in review time. The acceleration follows changes implemented in January, when MARAD assumed the lead role in deepwater port reviews and the U.S. Coast Guard shifted to a supporting role focused on vessel operations, maritime safety and security. ST LNG filed its application with MARAD and the Coast Guard on June 9, 2025. Under the streamlined approach, MARAD completed the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) in just 410 days. DOT credited the changes with eliminating unnecessary administrative procedures and accelerating the review process. In response to DOT’s announcement, gCaptain followed up with questions seeking additional insight into which specific changes had the greatest impact on reducing red tape. A DOT spokesperson, speaking on background, said “the primary efficiency gained was fixing a structural inefficiency, rather than addressing challenges within any specific partner agency.” Previously, MARAD and the U.S. Coast Guard operated under a co-lead structure for reviews required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). DOT’s spokesperson said this shared responsibility for environmental reviews “inadvertently created duplicative administrative steps, parallel document routing, and sequential reviews.” Now, with MARAD serving as the sole lead agency, project schedules have been consolidated and the review team has established a unified approach to interagency communication. “The U.S. Coast Guard remains an important partner in this process,” DOT explained, adding that “this shift simply allows them to focus purely on their core statutory missions of maritime safety, security, and operational risk assessment, while MARAD drives the environmental timeline.” The Coast Guard is listed in the project’s Record of Decision (ROD) as one of six federal cooperating agencies, but the document does not otherwise include or reference specific Coast Guard statements. Neither U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 6 nor the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, two other federal partners, filed objections or concerns regarding application approval. The deepwater port development will consist of four phases. Each phase includes five fixed offshore platforms (Gas Treatment, Liquefaction, Bridge Support Trestle, LNG Transfer, and Accommodation and Utilities), bridges linking the platforms, a dolphin mooring system composed of three berthing dolphins and six mooring dolphins, and a moored LNG Floating Storage Unit (FSU). At full build-out, the deepwater port will include 20 platforms, four FSUs, four mooring systems, and 7.7 miles of pipeline, consisting of a 5.6-mile lateral pipeline and 2.1 miles of interconnecting pipelines between the phases. DOT was asked whether the ST LNG project benefited from any one-time procedural exemptions that might not apply to future projects. DOT’s answer: No. Going forward, MARAD’s leadership role and the related procedural steps will follow the changes formally established in January. DOT was also asked to identify the types of red tape that have historically impeded timely reviews, such as repetitive filings or demands for unnecessary information. The spokesperson said the primary efficiency came from eliminating duplicative administrative procedures. Under the previous co-lead model, draft environmental documents, requests for information and legal reviews often had to move sequentially between multiple agencies before they could advance or be published. “By consolidating the NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act) process under MARAD,” DOT said, “we established a single Federal docket and a unified project management team. We eliminated redundant legal and administrative processing, aligned our public comment periods, and streamlined how cooperating agencies provide input.” Finally, DOT was asked about environmental reviews that must proceed according to nature’s timetable, such as studies involving temperature cycles, migration patterns or other seasonal factors. Were there opportunities to streamline reviews of environmental processes that inherently take weeks or months to evaluate? DOT replied: “Streamlining our administrative process does not mean cutting corners on rigorous environmental science or biological mandates.” To manage extended seasonal or biological studies efficiently, the spokesperson said MARAD is “front-loading” interagency coordination. MARAD’s team is engaging cooperating agencies, such as NOAA Fisheries, earlier in the scoping and pre-application phases to identify required biological studies as soon as possible. MARAD is also seeking to maximize the use of existing regional data from prior offshore projects to satisfy baseline requirements where appropriate, reducing the need for duplicative studies conducted from scratch. DOT noted that “when project-specific seasonal data collection is legally required, we integrate those study schedules into a predictable, concurrent review timeline rather than letting them cause cascading, sequential delays. This approach ensures we maintain the exact same statutory level of environmental assurance while drastically reducing idle administrative time in the schedule.” To be clear, MARAD’s application approval is not the same as the issuance of a license to operate. In fact, MARAD’s approval is conditional. ST LNG must agree in writing not to make changes to its deepwater port application and must demonstrate compliance with nine conditions before a license can be issued. Those conditions cover matters ranging from financial responsibility and oil spill liability to eventual decommissioning. The required compliance documentation must be submitted at least 90 days before a license can be issued. articles.summary: Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Artist’s rendering of the U.S. Navy’s planned Medium Landing Ship (LSM), designed to transport Marines, equipment and supplies in support of expeditionary operations. (Image: U.S. Navy) Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South Korean company’s push into U.S. naval shipbuilding. TOTE Services announced Friday that it selected Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) as the first shipbuilder under its $2.2 billion Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract for the LSM program. The award covers construction of one vessel at the Philadelphia shipyard, with options for three additional ships. Construction is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the program’s first vessel scheduled for delivery in 2030. The selection follows a competitive bidding process launched in July and comes just days after Hanwha announced plans to place its Philadelphia shipyard under the control of its U.S. defense subsidiary. “Since acquiring Philly Shipyard in 2024, Hanwha has made significant investments in its workforce and technology to pave the way to build ships for the U.S. Navy and other federal customers,” said HDUSA President and CEO Michael Coulter. The contract represents Hanwha Defense USA’s first U.S. Navy shipbuilding award and a significant step in the company’s effort to transform the former commercial shipyard into a dual-use facility serving both military and commercial customers. TOTE Services said Hanwha was selected based on its competitive pricing and acceptance of subcontract terms and conditions. The company is also continuing contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, which are expected to participate in construction of the LSM fleet. “This award shows the speed at which the VCM model can move from RFP to contract,” said TOTE Services President Jeff Dixon. “Through a competitive process, we secured strong terms that benefit the government, along with build positions that allow construction to start in the fourth quarter of 2027.” The LSM program is intended to provide the Marine Corps with smaller amphibious vessels capable of transporting personnel, equipment and supplies between islands and coastal locations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific. The Navy and Marine Corps are planning a fleet of 35 vessels, with TOTE’s initial contract covering up to eight ships. The award also builds on an existing relationship between TOTE Services and the Philadelphia yard. Under a separate VCM arrangement with the U.S. Maritime Administration, TOTE has overseen construction of the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) program at Philly Shipyard. Four of the five training ships have already been delivered. “Hanwha Philly Shipyard has already built and delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under the VCM model with TOTE Services, and we will leverage that experience to deliver the LSM to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps,” said Tim Glinatsis, senior vice president of program management at HDUSA. The announcement comes amid a broader restructuring of Hanwha’s U.S. shipbuilding operations. As gCaptain recently reported , Hanwha Defense USA announced this week that it is acquiring a controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard, shifting the facility toward defense-led ownership as the company expands its U.S. naval shipbuilding business. Hanwha acquired the shipyard in December 2024 and has since been investing in workforce development, infrastructure and technology to support an expansion into naval construction. The shift has also raised questions about the future balance between military and commercial shipbuilding at one of the country’s major Jones Act shipyards. Asked by gCaptain whether Hanwha would maintain and expand commercial Jones Act shipbuilding capacity as the yard transitions toward defense-led ownership, a company spokesperson said it was “in a good position to compete and build for commercial and naval demand as a dual-use yard.” Friday’s contract announcement provides the clearest indication yet of how Hanwha intends to put that strategy into practice, establishing a foothold in Navy ship construction while positioning the Philadelphia facility to compete for additional government and commercial work. articles.title: Grimaldi Warns U.S. Port Fees Could Force Ships Out of American Trades
articles.summary: Italian shipping giant Grimaldi Group is warning that reinstating U.S. port fees on foreign-built vehicle carriers could force it to redeploy vessels away from American trades, potentially disrupting shipping services...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Grimaldi Group Italian shipping giant Grimaldi Group is warning that reinstating U.S. port fees on foreign-built vehicle carriers could force it to redeploy vessels away from American trades, potentially disrupting shipping services for U.S. exporters and automakers. In an October 30 filing with the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) , Grimaldi strongly backed the Trump administration’s proposal to extend the suspension of Section 301 port fees through January 9, 2027. The company went a step further, calling for a permanent suspension of the fees targeting foreign-built vehicle carriers. “Many of our American customers have expressed concern at the thought of Grimaldi redeploying its ships out of US trades if the proposed further suspension of this Section 301 action is not implemented,” the company said. The warning comes as USTR considers a two-month extension of the existing suspension , which is scheduled to expire November 9. The proposed extension would keep the measures on hold through January 9, 2027, while Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. Grimaldi, one of the world’s largest operators of roll-on/roll-off, container and pure car and truck carriers, argued that the fees could have unintended consequences for American businesses that depend on its services. The company pointed to its cargo volumes over the past three years, reporting nearly 985,000 tons of U.S. exports and 1.31 million tons of imports. According to Grimaldi, 74.7% of its U.S. import volume consisted of cargo belonging to American automakers. In total, the company said 86% of the cargo it carries in U.S. trades consists of American exports or imports associated with U.S. automakers. “Few shipping lines have such a high percentage of American cargo,” Grimaldi said. The company also highlighted its longstanding relationship with the United States, noting that it has called at American ports since 2001 and supplied cargo ships to the U.S. Navy during the Second Gulf War. The filing adds to growing concerns among international shipping companies over the potential return of Section 301 fees, which were introduced last year as part of Washington’s effort to counter China’s dominance of the global maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors. The measures initially took effect on October 14, 2025, before being suspended on November 10 as part of a broader trade agreement between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The fees target Chinese-owned and Chinese-operated vessels, Chinese-built ships and certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. Although intended to strengthen American shipbuilding, the measures have faced criticism from carriers that argue they could increase transportation costs and disrupt established shipping networks. Grimaldi’s warning follows similar concerns raised by Atlantic Container Line (ACL), whose CEO Andy Abbott told gCaptain last week that customers feared the carrier would redeploy ships away from U.S. trades if the fees returned. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” Abbott said. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade.” The concerns from Grimaldi and ACL highlight a potential conflict between Washington’s efforts to rebuild domestic shipbuilding and the interests of American exporters that rely on foreign-built ships to move their cargo. The administration’s proposed extension has also faced opposition from lawmakers and maritime labor groups that want the fees reinstated. In June, Senators Mark Kelly and Elizabeth Warren urged USTR to restore the charges, arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild U.S. commercial shipbuilding and deprived the government of potential revenue for maritime investments. For Grimaldi, however, the issue goes beyond a temporary extension. The company is calling for permanent relief from the fees imposed under Annex III of the Section 301 action, which specifically addresses foreign-built vehicle carriers. “Grimaldi understands the intentions of USTR to advance policies that strengthen US national security and manufacturing/agricultural/maritime competitiveness,” the company said. But it added that it hopes “no insurmountable roadblocks will be put in our way.” The USTR public comment period closes October 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern Time. The proposed two-month extension has not yet been finalized.
