articles.body: TOTE Services Selects Hanwha Defense USA for Medium Landing Ship Program Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © TOTE Services TOTE Services, LLC, a U.S. maritime services company specializing in vessel construction management and ship management, announced its first shipyard selection, Hanwha Defense USA (HDUS), for the Medium Landing Ship (LSM) program under TOTE Services’ Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps. As VCM for the LSM program, TOTE Services issued a request for proposals (RFP) to qualified U.S. shipyards in July 2026. The award covers construction of one LSM, valued at $269 million, at Hanwha Philly Shipyard (HPSI), with options for three additional vessels. The program will include up to eight new vessels under the base contract. TOTE Services continues productive contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, both directed shipyards under the VCM contract, which are expected to play a meaningful role in building the LSM fleet. TOTE Services’ $2.2 billion VCM contract supports the Navy and Marine Corps’ planned 35-ship LSM fleet. The first vessel is expected to deliver in 2030. TOTE Services will provide one accountable management structure connecting government requirements to shipyard execution across three domestic shipbuilders, helping to accelerate delivery, strengthen cost and schedule discipline, and expand the U.S. shipbuilding industrial base. That work includes standardizing configuration across the fleet, using block buys to secure favorable pricing, and delivering vessels in a timely manner. TOTE Services pioneered the VCM model in U.S. government shipbuilding through its work on the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program for the U.S. Maritime Administration. As VCM for the five-vessel program, TOTE Services has overseen shipyard selection, design, construction, testing, delivery, and lifecycle logistics. Four vessels have been delivered, with the fifth, Golden State, expected in 2027. The LSM award builds on that work at Hanwha Philly Shipyard, where an experienced workforce and established supply chain position the yard to begin construction quickly. Beyond the ships themselves, the LSM program can provide a more reliable demand signal for American shipyards, suppliers, manufacturers and skilled trades, helping the industrial base plan, invest and build with greater consistency.

articles.summary: Dockworkers across 113 ports in 22 countries staged coordinated strikes and protests Friday, disrupting cargo operations and ferry services as part of a global campaign opposing arms shipments to Israel...

REUTERS/Louisa Gouliamaki/File Photo Dockworkers across 113 ports in 22 countries staged coordinated strikes and protests Friday, disrupting cargo operations and ferry services as part of a global campaign opposing arms shipments to Israel and the use of commercial ports for military logistics. The October 30 action, organized under the banner “Dockworkers Don’t Work for War,” involves more than 25 unions across five continents, with 24-hour strikes, shorter work stoppages and demonstrations at ports throughout Europe, the Mediterranean and beyond. Organizers describe the mobilization as the largest coordinated port action of its kind, estimating that approximately 52,000 containers carrying $2.8 billion worth of cargo could be delayed. The group puts the direct economic cost at $57 million, although those figures have not been independently verified. The largest disruptions are concentrated in France, Italy, Greece and Türkiye, where unions called 24-hour strikes. Additional work stoppages and demonstrations are taking place in Morocco, Cyprus and other countries, while Italy is also holding a general strike. In Greece, approximately 3,000 workers joined a walkout at the Port of Piraeus, disrupting cargo operations and ferry services, according to Reuters. The movement has also expanded beyond its traditional European and Mediterranean base, with actions in India, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Uruguay and the United States. On the U.S. West Coast, International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 10 is participating in actions in Oakland and San Francisco. Other participating unions include Germany’s ver.di, Sweden’s Svenska Hamnarbetarförbundet, Denmark’s 3F and the Maritime Union of Australia. Organizers have published an interactive map and list of participating ports , including major shipping hubs such as Valencia, Algeciras, Barcelona, Hamburg, Piraeus, Genoa and Tangier Med. Participation varies by location, ranging from full-day strikes to brief stoppages and solidarity demonstrations outside port gates. Not all participating ports are experiencing cargo disruptions. The campaign follows an earlier international day of action on February 6 involving 20 ports in seven countries, marking a significant expansion of coordinated labor opposition to the movement of military cargo through commercial shipping networks. The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has thrown its support behind the campaign, calling on governments and employers to respect workers’ rights to refuse military cargo without retaliation. “Governments must stop the flow of arms used to violate international humanitarian law,” said ITF General Secretary Stephen Cotton. “Governments and employers must respect the voice and rights of these workers.” The ITF said the protests are intended to challenge the movement of military equipment through civilian ports while also drawing attention to workers’ demands for better wages, improved working conditions and protections against increasing automation. ITF President Paddy Crumlin criticized governments for increasing military spending while workers face growing economic pressure. “Governments find billions for weapons while telling working people to accept insecure jobs, squeezed wages and increasing automation – dockers have every right to challenge this anti-worker agenda,” Crumlin said. The federation’s support builds on resolutions adopted at its 2024 Congress in Marrakech, where affiliated unions committed to calling for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza and measures to stop arms transfers contributing to violations of international humanitarian law. The campaign’s demands were further formalized in the Istanbul Declaration in May 2026, when unions representing more than 35 ports agreed to oppose the movement of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops through civilian port facilities. The protests are being supported by No Harbour for Genocide, an activist research organization that tracks military supply chains moving through commercial ports. According to the group, its research identified 315 shipments of components for Israeli defense manufacturer Elbit Systems passing through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries between August 2025 and September 2026. The organization also says it tracked approximately 3,400 shipments supplying U.S. military bases through 67 ports in 42 countries between December 2025 and September 2026. Organizers argue that coordinated action across multiple ports makes it more difficult for shipping companies to avoid disruptions by rerouting military cargo through alternative terminals. Previous dockworker actions have targeted individual shipments in Greece, France, Italy and Morocco, including efforts to block weapons and military components destined for Israel. The latest campaign seeks to expand those actions into a broader international movement opposing what participating unions describe as the militarization of civilian port infrastructure. The protests also come amid growing concerns about the safety of commercial seafarers operating in conflict zones. At Piraeus, Greek maritime unions linked the action to mounting casualties among merchant mariners in the Persian Gulf and Black Sea, where commercial vessels have faced missile, drone and other attacks. “We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons,” Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during Friday’s demonstration. Greek unions cited 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf during the first 21 days of October and 570 confirmed attacks in the Black Sea this year, which they said have killed 40 seafarers. Indian union representatives also raised concerns about casualties during the Iran war, saying approximately 15 Indian seafarers have died and others remain stranded by disruptions to maritime trade. Participating workers are demanding stronger safety protections, including access to medical personnel aboard vessels transiting war zones. The labor action comes as the shipping industry continues to grapple with attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz, growing insecurity in the Black Sea and wider geopolitical disruptions affecting major trade routes. Despite the scale of the mobilization, the actual impact on global shipping remains difficult to assess. Organizers say the participating ports collectively handle approximately 13.5% of global shipping activity and 63% of Mediterranean container activity. Those figures, however, reflect the ports’ overall share of trade rather than the volume of cargo directly affected by Friday’s actions. The estimated $2.8 billion in delayed cargo also represents goods potentially held up by the stoppages, rather than cargo lost or permanently removed from trade. For the participating unions, the objective extends beyond Friday’s operational disruptions. Organizers say further coordinated actions are planned as the international dockworkers’ movement continues to expand. articles.summary: A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was attacked by a small boat that attached two explosive devices to its hull, triggering an engine room fire and temporarily disabling the...

REUTERS/Stringer A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was attacked by a small boat that attached two explosive devices to its hull, triggering an engine room fire and temporarily disabling the vessel, according to a verified report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). The October 29 attack marks a significant escalation in the conflict, introducing a new threat to commercial shipping already facing repeated missile and drone strikes in and around the strategic waterway. According to UKMTO Warning 187-26, the incident occurred approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, as the tanker was transiting outbound from the strait. A small boat approached the tanker’s port side and attached two explosive devices above the waterline. The resulting explosions sparked a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabled the ship. UKMTO confirmed Friday that the crew was safe, the fire had been extinguished and there was no environmental impact. The tanker has since resumed its voyage. Maritime security sources identified the weapons as limpet mines, explosives attached directly to a vessel’s hull. The attack represents the first reported successful use of the tactic against merchant shipping in the waterway since the war began in February. Martin Kelly, Head of Advisory at EOS Risk Group, identified the vessel as the LOUISE 1 and said the attack marked another step in Iran’s evolving campaign against commercial shipping. He said the last time Iran used limpet mines against merchant shipping was in May 2019 when they attacked four vessels anchored off Fujairah and subsequent attacks on the tankers KOKUKA COURAGEOUS and FRONT ALTAIR in the Gulf of Oman the following month. The return of limpet mines adds another layer to the threat facing ships navigating the strait. Kelly warned that the implications could be particularly serious for vessels waiting at anchor, where explosives could potentially be placed below the waterline without being detected by the crew. “A limpet mine below the waterline will cause significant damage and water ingress,” he said. Multiple Attacks Reported as Iran Claims Three Tankers Hit The limpet-mine attack was one of several maritime security incidents reported in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. In a separate UKMTO warning, a company security officer reported that another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while completing an outbound transit of the strait at approximately 1600 UTC. No crew injuries or environmental impact were reported. Earlier Thursday, UKMTO also reported a vessel on fire approximately nine nautical miles north of Khasab. Regional authorities subsequently identified the vessel as a dhow that had been involved in a maritime security incident. The dhow caught fire, listed and sank. Its crew was safely evacuated, according to UKMTO. The incident follows an earlier U.S. military operation in which American forces reportedly destroyed a dhow suspected of providing intelligence to Iran. However, no connection between that operation and Thursday’s sinking has been established. Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy claimed Friday that three oil tankers had caught fire and exploded while attempting to transit routes it described as unauthorized. According to Iranian state media cited by Reuters, the IRGC claimed one tanker carrying approximately 2 million barrels of crude oil had struck a mine. Reuters said it could not independently verify the claims. Iran has repeatedly described attacks against ships using routes outside its control as mine strikes, but independent evidence supporting its broader claims of sea mines has remained limited. Attacks Concentrated Along Southern Transit Route The latest incidents come as the United States continues coordinating commercial vessel movements through the Strait of Hormuz, including a southern route intended to keep shipping moving despite Iranian threats. The route has increasingly become a focus of attacks. According to UKMTO’s October 30 weekly maritime security overview, 59 of 81 reported projectile strikes since July 6 occurred along the southern route. The report also highlighted the difficulty of establishing a complete picture of attacks across the region. “UKMTO reports only incidents verified through primary sources; additional incidents are known but cannot be independently verified,” the agency said. Since the conflict began on February 28, UKMTO has recorded 145 Iran-U.S. conflict-related incidents across its reporting area, including 88 incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz through October 28. Despite the continuing threat, commercial traffic has been recovering gradually. UKMTO reported 122 outbound and 155 inbound transits over its latest seven-day reporting period, up from 114 outbound and 127 inbound the previous week. However, combined traffic remains approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO also noted that around 80% of transits reported by U.S. Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping involve energy carriers. The latest attacks underscore the challenges facing efforts to restore normal shipping through the waterway. While military operations have focused heavily on missiles, drones and the threat of naval mines, the use of explosives placed directly onto a merchant vessel’s hull introduces another risk for operators. articles.summary: StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence…
articles.body: Portchain Acquired by StormGeo, Advancing Just-in-Time Voyage Optimization Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 Just-In Time port call coordination with Portchain. © Portchain/StormGeo StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence, creating the foundation for a new approach to Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale. The goal is to connect decisions about route and speed with the latest information on berth availability and terminal plans, helping operators respond to changes while a vessel is still at sea. Portchain connects container carriers and terminals through shared operational data. Portchain Connect supports digital alignment of vessel schedules and cargo volumes, while Portchain Quay supports berth, crane and workforce planning in a shared, real-time environment. Today, the Portchain Network connects shipping lines with more than 200 terminals, representing over 40% of global container terminal capacity. StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence combines voyage optimization, vessel-performance insight and expert route guidance to help operators optimize for arrival time, fuel consumption or the balance between the two. Portchain adds a shared, real-time view of berth plans aligned with terminal operators and their resources. As the companies develop this combined offering, a change in the expected berth time could inform speed decisions while the vessel is still at sea. Operators could reassess the voyage plan and better align the vessel’s estimated time of arrival (ETA) with its estimated time of berthing (ETB). Updated arrival information will also help terminals plan berths, cranes and teams. This is the foundation for Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale: turning a change in the terminal plan into a timely voyage decision. The aim is to help vessels arrive closer to when the terminal is ready to receive them, reducing avoidable waiting, fuel use and emissions while making arrivals more predictable. The acquisition advances StormGeo’s ambition to connect weather, vessel and port insights in support of more efficient and predictable maritime operations. Together with Alfa Laval’s marine portfolio, it supports customers’ efforts to improve operational efficiency and progress towards decarbonization. The addition also strengthens Alfa Laval’s offering across the fuel transition and energy efficiency by adding StormGeo’s expertise in routing and port call coordination, with digitalization and AI helping to simplify maritime operations. Portchain will operate as an independent company under StormGeo for the next few years and will later be fully integrated into StormGeo’s portfolio. Existing Portchain customers will see no disruption to their service, and the combined offering will be available through StormGeo.

articles.body: Business & Finance October 30, 2026 · 7 hours ago Mazarine taking the helm at Black Sea Oil & Gas as Carlyle and EBRD exit Mazarine Energy has struck a deal to acquire Romania's largest offshore gas producer, Black Sea Oil & Gas (BSOG). MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Vadu Gas Treatment Plant (GTP Vadu) operated by Black Sea Oil & Gas as part of the Midia Gas Development (MGD) project near Vadu in Constanța County, Romania. articles.title: ClassNK Releases Second Edition of Cyber Security Management Guidelines
articles.summary: ClassNK has released the second edition of its "Guidelines for Cyber Security Management System for Ships." Intended for shipowners and ship management companies, the guidelines set out the requirements for a Cyber Security Management System (CSMS)…
articles.body: ClassNK Releases Second Edition of Cyber Security Management Guidelines Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © ClassNK ClassNK has released the second edition of its "Guidelines for Cyber Security Management System for Ships." Intended for shipowners and ship management companies, the guidelines set out the requirements for a Cyber Security Management System (CSMS), through which a Company addresses the cyber risks associated with ship operations as part of its day-to-day work, from governance and responsibilities ashore and onboard to the technical controls applied to shipboard systems. The Guidelines also make ClassNK’s certification audits transparent by showing the assessment criteria applied in them. In audits, ClassNK looks at the governance behind a company’s cyber security: policy and management commitment, defined roles and responsibilities, risk assessment, implementation and operation of controls, and preparedness for incidents. The second edition has been restructured with reference to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002, and the assessment criteria for each CSMS requirement have been clarified. The requirements have also been mapped to the cyber security requirements of major vetting schemes. Cyber security is increasingly covered in the external assessments conducted by maritime stakeholders, and many of those requirements focus on how cyber risk is managed. A CSMS certified against these guidelines gives companies an objective means of demonstrating that governance to external stakeholders, and a single foundation for responding to multiple vetting requirements. Background The IMO recommends that cyber risks be managed within the Safety Management Systems under the ISM Code. In response, ClassNK published the first edition of the Guidelines in 2019, setting out CSMS requirements built on the framework of the ISM Code, and has since been providing CSMS certification based on the guidelines. As a collective effort of the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS), the application of IACS UR E26 and E27 has defined the cyber resilience capabilities that ships and their onboard systems must have from the newbuild phase. At the same time, a vessel’s operating environment keeps changing throughout its service life, as the systems are updated and operations and organizations change. Addressing cyber risks is therefore not a matter of technical measures alone; continuous management is essential to select, implement, maintain and review those measures appropriately. In recent years, cyber risk management covering practices such as access control, software updates, education and training, and incident response have also become a part of the assessment criteria as part of the subject to the schemes established by DryBMS, OCIMF, RightShip and others, each with their own criteria. The first edition offered the elements for establishing a CSMS as a high-level objective, leaving each Company to interpret how to achieve them within its own organization. Putting those elements into practice requires wide efforts across the whole Company, from shore-based organizations to shipboard operations, and time to achieve. Through its audits since 2019, ClassNK has built up practical knowledge of what effective implementation looks like. Drawing on that experience, the second edition makes clear what is verified in audits and has been designed with other external assessments in mind, so that a CSMS built on the guidelines also prepares a company to meet them. Main revisions Clarification of audit criteria, structured with reference to international standards The guidelines now consist of two parts: Part 1 sets out the CSMS requirements, and Part 2 specifies the audit criteria and the objective evidence required for each requirement. This allows companies to understand in advance what will be verified in audits and prepare accordingly, and makes it easier to identify where there is room for improvement in their own practices. Mapping to external assessment criteria set by major industry bodies The assessment criteria in Part 2 have also been mapped against the cyber security requirements or benchmarks of major vetting bodies (covering RISQ, SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA*3). Rather than interpreting each scheme separately, Companies can use the CSMS as a common framework for meeting them and can expect the reduction of the time and burden needed for compliance. ClassNK will continue to support cyber security efforts in the maritime industry through the provision of guidelines as well as audits and certification. How to access guidelines The guidelines are available to download via "Guidelines" of My Page on ClassNK’s website after registration: ClassNK MyPage Login

articles.body: Corn Belt Ports See Notable Freight Tonnage Growth in 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © Corn Belt Ports In the most recent annual report released by the U.S. Waterborne Commerce Statistics Center, two Corn Belt Ports regions took top honors for showing some of the highest growth rates in the inland waterway port system. The Mid-America Port Commission (IL, MO, IA), established in 1999, was ranked as the 40th largest port in the U.S., and saw a 15.2% growth in freight tonnage during the 2024 reporting year (published 2026). This is the highest growth rate for any large (Top 50) U.S. Inland Port. The Illinois Waterway Ports Commission established in 2023, and now reported as a port statistical area in the report, saw a 5.9% increase in freight tonnage, the largest increase of any port statistical area in the U.S. In the report the Upper Mississippi River (Marine Highway 35) saw a 4.2% increase, and the Illinois River (Marine Highway 55 NORTH) saw a 1.2% increase in freight tonnage overall. The Corn Belt Ports are special districts of government or official government collaborations. They are the modern, sustainable, rural, regional, inland, partnership ports on the Upper Mississippi River (Marine Highway 35) and the Illinois River (Marine Highway 35 NORTH) inside of the lock and dam system recognized by the U.S. Congress as the Upper Mississippi River and Illinois Waterway System. The Corn Belt Ports consist of the Illinois Waterway Ports Commission, the Mid-America Port Commission, the Upper Mississippi River Ports of Eastern lowa and Western Illinois, and the Northern Grain Belt Ports. articles.summary: Turkish shipbuilder Sanmar Shipyards has delivered a new harbour tugboat to Bulgarian operator VTC S.A., marking the fifth vessel supplied to the company since their partnership began in 2003.The tug, renamed KASTRITSI by its new owner, will join VTC's fleet at the Black Sea port of Varna…
articles.body: Sanmar Hands Over New Harbour Tug for Bulgaria's Black Sea Port Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 KASTRITSI tug (Credit: Sanmar Shipyards) Turkish shipbuilder Sanmar Shipyards has delivered a new harbour tugboat to Bulgarian operator VTC S.A., marking the fifth vessel supplied to the company since their partnership began in 2003. The tug, renamed KASTRITSI by its new owner, will join VTC's fleet at the Black Sea port of Varna, supporting harbour towage and marine operations. Based on the RApport 2500 design by Robert Allan, KASTRITSI is a shallow-draft Azimuth Stern Drive (ASD) tug designed for operations in confined and shallow waterways. The vessel measures 25.2 meters in length and 12 meters in beam, with a maximum draught of 4.2 meters, ahead bollard pull exceeding 50 tonnes and a maximum speed of 12 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi-1 firefighting capability and accommodation for six crew members. Sanmar's engagement with VTC dates back to 2003, when the shipbuilder supplied three twin-screw tugs, SANMAR XII, SANMAR XIII and SANMAR XIV. A fourth tug, TICHA, based on Robert Allan's RApport 1600SX design, followed in 2018. "We have been working with VTC since the very beginning of its operations in 2003, and we are proud of the relationship we have built over more than two decades. The delivery of KASTRITSI marks another important step in our cooperation, and we are delighted to see her join the VTC fleet in Varna," said Cem Seven, Chairman of Sanmar Shipyards. VTC provides harbour towage and marine services in the Bulgarian ports of Varna and Balchik, including vessel assistance, berthing and unberthing, coastal and offshore towage, and emergency response.

articles.body: General Dynamics' Backlog Surges to $220B on Major Defense Orders Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 (Credit: General Dynamics) General Dynamics reported $98.8 billion in new orders in the third quarter of 2026, driven by major submarine contracts, while revenue rose 12.9% year-on-year to $14.6 billion, the company announced on October 30. The aerospace and defense company's total backlog reached $220.3 billion at the end of the quarter, with an additional $50.4 billion in estimated potential contract value, bringing its total estimated contract value to $270.7 billion. Orders across its defense segments totaled $93.8 billion, driven by large contracts for Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines in its Marine Systems business, while the Aerospace segment secured $5 billion in orders. The company's book-to-bill ratio, which measures orders received relative to revenue, reached 6.8 for the quarter, including 8.5 across its defense segments and 1.4 in Aerospace. General Dynamics reported operating earnings of $1.5 billion, up 14.7% from the same period last year, while diluted earnings per share increased 15.7% to $4.49. Operating margin improved by 20 basis points to 10.5%. “Our business had exceptional third quarter results, with revenue growth across all four segments, robust bookings and solid operational performance,” said Phebe Novakovic, chairman and chief executive officer of General Dynamics. “With the consistent growth in our backlog and our significant investment in our businesses over the last decade, we are poised to drive continued performance in the years to come.” Cash from operating activities totaled $1.7 billion, representing 139% of net earnings. During the quarter, General Dynamics invested $481 million in capital expenditures, paid $429 million in dividends and reduced its total debt by $500 million. The company ended the quarter with $7 billion in total debt and $4.4 billion in cash and equivalents.

articles.summary: The Baltic Exchange has received two whistleblowing claims of attempted manipulation of the world’s benchmark tanker rate since the beginning of the war in Iran, according to documents made public as part of a major legal battle with trading house Mercuria Energy Group.

REUTERS/Toby Melville/Files By Alex Longley and Jack Farchy Oct 30, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The Baltic Exchange has received two whistleblowing claims of attempted manipulation of the world’s benchmark tanker rate since the beginning of the war in Iran, according to documents made public as part of a major legal battle with trading house Mercuria Energy Group. The manipulation allegations are likely to heap further scrutiny on the rate, known as TD3C, which is the world’s most important benchmark for the cost of chartering oil tankers and on which billions of dollars of derivatives and other contracts depend. In the legal case, hearings for which began in London this week, Mercuria is arguing that the Baltic should have suspended the TD3C rate from Saudi Arabia to China after the war in Iran broke out this year. So far, while Mercuria has argued that the TD3C index was not representative of reality, it hasn’t made any suggestion that it was being manipulated. One of the claims of alleged manipulation was against Mercuria itself, alongside another company that was not identified. The Baltic’s investigation of that claim did not establish that the benchmark had been manipulated, according to the Baltic’s written opening arguments and a witness statement from its head of compliance. A second claim of manipulation, against another unnamed company, is still under investigation, the Baltic’s filings showed. Mercuria’s lawyers said in written opening arguments that it “strongly and categorically rejects any allegation of wrongdoing.” They argued that the allegations were “irrelevant” to the trial. The prices published by the Baltic Exchange are set by assessments received from panels of shipbrokers, who sign up to a code of conduct based on the motto “our word our bond.” However, since the Iran war it has become significantly harder to establish the reality of which ships are being hired to transport oil through the Strait of Hormuz and at what price. The number of shipments plummeted in the months following the outbreak of the war, and those that did take place were mostly shrouded in secrecy. Brokers have been left parsing extremely limited information to assess the benchmark rate. Bloomberg has reported that, in recent months, WhatsApp messages sent by shipping tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung’s Sinokor Group have become one of the main drivers of the price. Middle East to China tanker earnings have surged from $218,000 a day before the war to $1.35 million on Thursday. Read: The Tanker Tycoon’s WhatsApps Driving a Disputed Oil Benchmark Going in to the war, Mercuria had large short positions in derivatives linked to TD3C, according to its filings in the case, which it used to hedge the earnings of its fleet of tankers. It accounted for between a quarter and a half of the open interest in TD3C derivatives, according to a witness statement from one of its freight traders. After the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28 and the transit of ships through the Strait of Hormuz became nearly impossible, Mercuria suffered because the price of TD3C soared, resulting in losses on its derivatives positions, while its tankers weren’t able to transit Hormuz and take advantage of soaring rates. The complaint alleging manipulation by Mercuria was sent to the Baltic by a whistleblower by email on April 24, according to the witness statement of the group’s head of compliance, Abisade Aluko. It concerned a reported agreement involving Mercuria that was circulated to brokers on March 17, for the charter of a tanker at 350 industry-standard Worldscale points, well below the published TD3C rate at the time, according to Aluko. A separate witness statement from Mercuria freight trader Renaud Hauspy showed that the vessel, the Yasa Southern Cross, was hired from Mercuria by TotalEnergies SE, though he didn’t specify the rate. The Baltic’s freight assessor on that day said the agreement “feels a bit ‘strange’” as it was privately negotiated and both companies involved had significant derivatives positions, according to the Baltic’s lawyers. Two of the Baltic’s assessors later told Aluko that they felt Mercuria and another unnamed company “were trying to manipulate the market,” according to Aluko’s witness statement. A representative from Total declined to comment. Hauspy offered a possible explanation of the relatively low rate, saying that the agreement contained an option for the ship to load either inside the Persian Gulf at the port of Ras Tanura or outside it at Fujairah, depending on the security situation. Ultimately it had loaded at Fujairah, he said. Hauspy said that from the middle of March he began trying to hire out some of Mercuria’s vessels for journeys beginning inside the Persian Gulf, but that doing so was “impossible.” He said that by the middle of April, the company was making almost daily unsolicited offers to each of its shipbroker contacts for vessels to load in the Persian Gulf and progressively lowered the rate for those ships over time in a bid to secure a booking. The rates, which ranged from 400 Worldscale points in mid-April to 300 Worldscale points by mid-June, were substantially below the Baltic’s published rates at the time of between 391 and 480 Worldscale points. In court, James McClelland, a lawyer for the Baltic, argued that the string of April offers began just days before the company filed its claim against the pricing agency and that a lower rate would benefit positions Mercuria had that were tied to the world’s main tanker index. He added that the company knew its ships wouldn’t be able to enter the Persian Gulf, as the owners wouldn’t give permission to enter Hormuz. Hauspy said that the reasoning behind the company making the offers was purely commercial and that there was a very strong commercial incentive to hire out ships inside the Persian Gulf where possible as a result of the surge in tanker rates. articles.summary: A small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel, in the first successful use of such explosives in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said on Friday.

Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Oct 30 (Reuters) – A small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel, in the first successful use of such explosives in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said on Friday. The crew was safe, there was no environmental impact and the fire had been extinguished, British navy agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said in an advisory note, adding that the vessel, which it did not name, was continuing to its next port of call. The incident occurred on Thursday, 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman’s Khasab, UKMTO said. It was not immediately clear who was behind the attack. The incident comes amid repeated attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important oil export routes, since the outbreak of the conflict between the US and Iran in February. Iran has hit vessels it says have violated its restrictions on passage through the strategic waterway, as it seeks to assert control over the strait and exert pressure on Washington. The tanker — the Panama-flagged Louise 1 — was targeted with limpet mines, according to assessments from three maritime security sources. This is the first known successful strike using limpet mines in the area since the beginning of the US war with Iran and followed a separate attempt in September using such devices which did not detonate, two of the sources said. “The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait’s congested shipping lanes,” Greece-based maritime risk management group Marisks said in a note on Friday. Marisks said limpet mines were first deployed in the region in 2017 and used against tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in subsequent years, adding that “limpet mines are cheap and easily available.” “The methodology of a small craft attaching these mines on the hulls of vessels in transit is cheap, low tech and very efficient,” it said. Ukrainian forces also hit the Louise 1 in July with naval drones in the Black Sea over what Ukraine’s SBU security service said was its role in transporting Russian oil and being part of the so-called shadow fleet of tankers deployed by Moscow to keep oil exports flowing. The vessel’s Panama-based operator, listed in shipping databases as Aquarius Maritime Ventures, could not be immediately reached for comment. articles.title: Noble rigs’ $560 million drilling gigs push fleet backlog to $6.7 billion
articles.summary: Noble Corporation has secured a string of new deals across multiple geographies, spanning South America, Africa, and Europe.
articles.body: Contracts & Tenders October 30, 2026 · 11 hours ago Noble rigs’ $560 million drilling gigs push fleet backlog to $6.7 billion Noble Corporation has secured a string of new deals across multiple geographies, spanning South America, Africa, and Europe. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Noble Intrepid jack-up rig Source: Noble Corporation U.S.-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Noble Corporation is fueling its fleet utilization uptick with multimillion-dollar drilling assignments off the coasts of Uruguay, Nigeria, Ghana, Peru, and Norway, enabling its total contract backlog to hit $6.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. With new contract wins of approximately $560 million awarded since the July fleet status report, Noble’s backlog as of October 26, 2026, stands at $6.7 billion, excluding mobilization and demobilization revenue. The firm's fleet of 23 marketed floaters was 66% contracted during the third quarter compared with 64% in the prior quarter, while recent contract awards added around 44 months of new floater backlog, with leading edge day rates for Tier-1 drillships ranging between the mid-$400,000s and $500,000. The utilization of Noble's five marketed ultra-harsh jack-ups was 86% in the third quarter versus 80% during the prior quarter, while latest contract awards brought approximately 26 months of new jack-up backlog, with leading edge day rates ranging between $230,000 and $300,000. " The third quarter, which featured a 5% sequential decrease in adjusted EBITDA, marked the successful resumption of operations for both of our rigs in Brazil, but was also impacted by several other rigs across the fleet transitioning between contracts. On the commercial front, we have recently secured approximately $560 million in new contract awards, including a number of key programs that support a strengthening fleet utilization profile as we move through 2027. " — Robert Eifler Noble's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) The 2014-built Noble BlackHawk drillship has secured one-well contract with Apache Corporation in Uruguay , which is expected to begin in Q4 2027, with an estimated duration of 50 days. This contract award of approximately $25 million excludes additional fees for mobilization and demobilization. The 2014-built Noble BlackRhino drillship has landed a four-well deal with TotalEnergies in Nigeria , which is anticipated to start in Q4 2026, with an estimated duration of 150 days plus six priced option wells. The 2013-built Noble Faye Kozack drillship has won a five-well assignment with Tullow Oil in Ghana , which is slated to commence in mid-2027, with an estimated duration of 250 days. This contract also comes with five priced option wells. The 2011-built Noble Globetrotter I drillship has picked up a two-well contract with Oxy in Peru , which is scheduled to kick off in Q2 2027. Terms of the contract, which includes additional fees for mobilization and demobilization, are not disclosed. Afterward, this rig is expected to embark on its contract with TotalEnergies in West Africa under a three-year capacity reservation agreement (CRA) for light well intervention services, providing a minimum commitment of 150 days per year, with first call-off service order set to start in Angola in Q3/Q4 2027. The 2014-built Noble Interceptor jack-up rig has obtained a one-well contract with DNO in Norway , which is anticipated to begin in Q3 2027, with an estimated duration of 50-90 days. As a result, the rig is expected to kick off, in direct continuation, a long-term plug and abandonment (P&A) scope for ConocoPhillips in Norway on the Ekofisk field , with an estimated duration of 670 days. The 2014-built Noble Intrepid jack-up rig has been hired on a one-well assignment with Orlen in Norway, which is due to commence in Q3 2027, with an estimated duration of 40-60 days. " Forward contract coverage and dayrate trends for both deepwater and ultra-harsh environment jack-ups continue to methodically improve, despite limited apparent demand tailwinds arising from higher oil prices during 2026 thus far. Noble's recent contract fixtures encompass a diversity of customers and regions, spanning frontier exploration to late-cycle well operations. We continue to build backlog that supports an expected meaningful inflection in fleet utilization and cash flow starting H2 2027, with already approximately 20% more contracted capacity in our fleet in H2 2027 compared to H1 2027. articles.body: Europe Greater China Shipyards Tankers Swedish owner Veritas books up to six chemical tankers in China Adis Ajdin October 30, 2026 0 853 1 minute read Nantong Rainbow Offshore & Engineering Equipment Nantong Rainbow Offshore & Engineering Equipment Swedish shipowner Veritas Tankers has placed an order for up to six 13,000 dwt stainless steel chemical tankers at China’s Nantong Rainbow Offshore & Engineering Equipment, in a deal potentially worth $248m. The yard’s Shenzhen-listed parent, Jiangsu Rainbow Heavy Industries, confirmed the contract with an unnamed European owner in a stock exchange filing, putting the total value of the six-ship package, including options, at CNY1.5bn to CNY1.65bn ($225m to $248m). Shipbroking sources identify Sweden’s Rederi AB Veritas Tankers as the buyer, although the shipowner has not publicly confirmed its involvement. Rainbow has withheld the customer’s identity on commercial confidentiality grounds. The Chinese group has not specified how many vessels are firm and how many remain optional, but said deliveries are scheduled to begin 28 months after the contract is signed. The newbuildings are intended for parcel chemical trades, with designs suited to restricted waterways and operating conditions in northern Europe. For Rainbow, the deal adds another European customer to its chemical tanker business. The Nantong yard previously secured a contract from Germany’s John T. Essberger for two firm 13,000 dwt stainless steel chemical tankers and four options, with deliveries starting in 2027. That programme, covered by Splash in September 2024, forms part of Essberger’s fleet renewal drive and its investment in the E&S Tankers Pool operated with Stolt Tankers. Since 2022, Ove Johnsson has wholly owned and controlled Veritas Tankers. The company operates a fleet of five chemical tankers. Dajin disclosed that the option under a three-plus-one shipbuilding agreement signed in July had expired and that the Greek customer had elected not to proceed after discussions between the parties. The three firm ships, valued at a combined CNY1.575bn (about $235m), remain on order at subsidiary Tangshan Dajin, with completion scheduled across 2029 and 2030. The original deal carried a maximum value of CNY2.1bn ($313m) if the additional ship was declared. The yard said the decision does not constitute a contractual breach or trigger penalties. Dajin also expects no material impact on its production schedule or 2026 financial performance. The Chinese group did not identify the customer in its filing. However, Chinese shipbuilding market reports have linked the contract to Kriton Lendoudis-led Evalend Shipping. Splash covered the original agreement in July when Evalend emerged as the reported buyer of the three-plus-one series, marking the Greek owner’s entry into the newcastlemax sector. The group has since been linked to further tanker and bulk carrier investments in Asia, including a quartet of LR1 product tankers at Yangzijiang Shipbuilding. Other Greek owners have also turned to Dajin for newcastlemax tonnage. John Coustas-led Danaos Corporation has four 211,000 dwt vessels on order for delivery in 2028, while the Adrianopoulos family’s Cape Shipping has booked a pair of the same size for 2029 in a deal worth around $153m. articles.title: €3.1 billion Spain-France interconnector is 70% complete
articles.summary: The multibillion-euro Biscay Gulf interconnector, set to increase electricity exchange capacity between Spain and France from 2.8 GW to 5 GW, is...
articles.body: Interconnectors October 30, 2026 · 13 hours ago €3.1 billion Spain-France interconnector is 70% complete NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Red Eléctrica The multibillion-euro Biscay Gulf interconnector, set to increase electricity exchange capacity between Spain and France from 2.8 GW to 5 GW, is 70% complete, with onshore cable laying currently underway. Spanish transmission system operator (TSO) Red Eléctrica has begun underground cable laying for the electrical interconnection project that will, across the Bay of Biscay, connect Gatika in Spain and France's Cubnezais. The underground HVDC cables will run for 13 kilometers, from the Gatika converter station to the coast at Lemoiz, where they will connect to the submarine cables. Furthermore, Red Eléctrica recently completed the second phase of subsea cable laying, a 50-kilometer stretch, using Prysmian's cable-laying vessel (CLV) Monna Lisa. On the Biscayan coast, the first phase was completed in August with NKT's CLV Victoria, which was responsible for installing the first 65 kilometers of the route. With this, all the submarine cables have been installed in the Biscay section of the submarine interconnection. Work will continue on the sections off the coast of Gipuzkoa between November and February, with all sections expected to be laid in French waters until the summer. The Spanish TSO also reported that the construction of the future Gatika converter station is progressing well, with civil engineering work completed and the electromechanical assembly currently underway. The Biscay Gulf interconnector is now 70% complete. Developed by Red Eléctrica and its French counterpart RTE, through the joint venture Inelfe, the project is considered a Project of Common Interest by the European Union and is co-financed through CINEA - the European Union's Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, in addition to support from the European Investment Bank (EIB). articles.title: Dockworkers unite across 113 ports in global anti-war protest
articles.summary: One of the largest coordinated port labour mobilisations in history is underway today, with more than 25 unions staging strikes and demonstrations at 113 ports across 22 countries and territories. The worldwide action, organised under the banner “Dockworkers do not work for war”, has expanded dramatically from a...
articles.body: Ports and Logistics Dockworkers unite across 113 ports in global anti-war protest Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 1,684 1 minute read CGT CGT One of the largest coordinated port labour mobilisations in history is underway today, with more than 25 unions staging strikes and demonstrations at 113 ports across 22 countries and territories. The worldwide action, organised under the banner “Dockworkers do not work for war”, has expanded dramatically from a smaller mobilisation involving 20 ports across seven countries in February. Major gateways involved include Hamburg, Le Havre, Marseille, Genoa, Gioia Tauro, Piraeus, Tangier Med, Mersin and India’s Nhava Sheva. France’s CGT has called a 24-hour walkout across approximately 24 ports, predicting that as much as 95% of national port activity could be halted. Italy has registered a nationwide 24-hour ports strike, coinciding with a general strike affecting other transport sectors. In Greece, seafarers’ unions have called 24-hour stoppages expected to disrupt ferry services at Piraeus, Rafina, Lavrio, Patras and Igoumenitsa. Organisers estimate that participating unions represent workers handling around 40% of Mediterranean container traffic, with up to 40,000 containers potentially delayed.< However, the actual disruption remains uncertain. Some ports are holding demonstrations rather than stopping cargo operations, while Genoa’s port authority anticipates relatively limited disruption. The campaign primarily opposes military cargo shipments through civilian ports, alongside demands for improved wages, working conditions and protections against automation. Although unprecedented in scale for this particular campaign, claims that it is the world’s largest port strike remain unverified. An international solidarity campaign for Liverpool dockworkers in January 1997 involved 105 ports and cities across 27 countries. No further worldwide coordinated strike date has been announced. Separately, a potential November 1 strike involving 250 port watchmen threatens operations at Los Angeles and Long Beach, although negotiations to avert the stoppage are continuing. Italy also faces another national general strike on November 20. articles.title: Oil majors count the cost of runaway tanker rates
articles.summary: Soaring tanker freight rates are taking an increasingly heavy toll on the world’s oil majors, with the latest quarterly results revealing billions of dollars in additional shipping-related liabilities, squeezed refining margins and losses on trading positions. Shell has disclosed a $5.4bn non-cash increase in its...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Oil majors count the cost of runaway tanker rates Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 1,803 2 minutes read Shell Shell Soaring tanker freight rates are taking an increasingly heavy toll on the world’s oil majors, with the latest quarterly results revealing billions of dollars in additional shipping-related liabilities, squeezed refining margins and losses on trading positions. Shell has disclosed a $5.4bn non-cash increase in its shipping lease liabilities during the third quarter, reflecting the extraordinary rise in tanker rates since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict. The accounting adjustment relates to index-linked vessel charters, which must be revalued using prevailing spot rates. Shell’s shipping lease liabilities have increased by nearly $7.7bn since the beginning of the year, although the company stressed that the revaluations do not represent immediate cash expenditure. Oil majors: VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their ten-year average Shell chief financial officer Sinead Gorman said freight rates between the Middle East and China were now around ten times their levels a year ago. “You see that starting to come into margins,” she told analysts, adding that higher transportation costs were affecting refining, chemicals and crude trading. The British major nevertheless reported adjusted third-quarter earnings of $10.8bn, more than double the year-earlier figure, benefiting from exceptionally strong refining margins. At TotalEnergies, chief executive Patrick Pouyanné revealed that shipping costs, previously around $2 to $3 per barrel, had climbed to approximately $25 per barrel. Pouyanné attributed around $6 per barrel of pressure on the company’s liquids price realisations to additional freight costs. The French major has some protection through its chartering strategy, with fixed-rate medium- and long-term agreements covering approximately 40% of the equity crude it lifts. Pouyanné said having tankers available at agreed rates had also allowed the company’s traders to profit from moving Iraqi crude through the Strait of Hormuz. Italian energy giant Eni has similarly acknowledged that rising shipping costs are eating into its refining earnings The company reported third-quarter refining adjusted operating profit of €730m, supported by strong margins and increased refinery utilisation, but said the gains were partly offset by higher freight costs and unfavourable crude differentials. Eni executive Pino Ricci confirmed that the company’s refining margin calculations incorporated the sharp increase in transportation costs resulting from the Hormuz crisis. Norway’s Equinor has reported a more direct trading impact. Its crude, products and liquids business swung to an adjusted operating loss of $96m in the third quarter, compared with a $355m profit in the preceding three months. Equinor attributed the deterioration to losses on derivative positions in the exceptionally tight shipping market, which more than offset strong products trading. The Norwegian major also identified increased freight rates as an important contributor to higher operating expenses during the first nine months of 2026. Oil majors hoping for some freight rate reprieve would have been disappointed with the bullish mood at this week’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco where tanker owners appeared in no hurry to call the top of the market. Arrow researcher Burak Cetinok calculated that VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their ten-year average, with the weekly multiple approaching 20, but saw no immediate sell signal. DHT Holdings chief executive Svein Moxnes Harfjeld argued that fleet ageing would help underpin the market. By the end of 2029, almost half the VLCC fleet will be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating substantial replacement requirements. Alberta Shipmanagement’s Alexia Inglessis pointed to recovering Middle Eastern oil flows, stronger Chinese demand, depleted inventories and sanctions-related inefficiencies. “I think we have a lot of things that point to a good market for the short to medium term,” she said. Speaking at the Money and Ships session of this week’s Maritime CEO Forum at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Christoph Toepfer, chief executive of Borealis Maritime, warned that shipping was “living on borrowed time” as conflicts and trade disruptions continue to inflate tonne-mile demand. “I always enjoy staying late at the party,” Toepfer said, before suggesting that the resolution of geopolitical crises could rapidly unwind some of the demand supporting today’s markets. Andy Dacy, CEO and CIO of JP Morgan Asset Management’s Global Transportation Group, was more optimistic, suggesting shipping had another 12 to 18 months of strong earnings ahead. “We’re on a plateau of some sort for at least the foreseeable future,” he said. Dacy pointed to the enormous number of vessels delivered between 2004 and 2012 that will approach recycling age over the coming years, providing a potential counterweight to any reduction in geopolitical disruption. “We have at least another 12 to 18 months of good times ahead of us based on bad things, of course,” he observed. CTM chief executive Carlos Pena was less convinced about current tanker valuations, suggesting owners should consider selling VLCCs at today’s elevated prices while remaining invested in dry bulk, which has yet to enjoy comparable earnings. The discussion, moderated by TURTLE chief executive Isabelle Rickmers, also revealed sharply contrasting definitions of successful investment. Toepfer recalled turning a $10m investment in a containership into $37m before reinvesting the proceeds in two large anchor handlers, subsequently sold for $130m. Pena argued that sometimes the best investment decision was accepting substantial losses early. Closing expensive charter positions had allowed CTM to survive and develop its pool operations. “You need to have courage and lose money,” Pena said. Massimo Giovannini, managing partner of TST Group, agreed, recalling his decision not to buy six Korean-built handysizes at approximately $17m apiece in 2014, ahead of years of depressed dry bulk earnings. Despite expectations of another downturn, the panellists were divided over whether shipping would experience another genuine financial crisis. Toepfer argued that strong balance sheets, abundant cash and low leverage would prevent widespread distress, with investors ready to acquire vessels whenever prices weakened. “I don’t think we will see a proper distressed market in the next 10 years,” he said, suggesting listed shipping companies might offer greater discounts than privately owned vessels during the next downturn. Dacy was more cautious, predicting a downturn within five years while highlighting how shipping’s reduced borrowing requirements had insulated it from intensifying competition for capital. “AI is sucking up capital across the board,” he warned, although shipowners currently have sufficient cash to repay debt rather than seek additional financing. Pena stressed that financing remained available for attractive projects but advised newcomers to shipping to gain experience before committing capital at today’s prices. The panellists also identified protectionism, a possible Taiwan crisis and speculative newbuilding orders as major threats, particularly unfixed containerships and car carriers scheduled for delivery several years from now.
